The failure is load-dependent: it succeeds on an idle host and fails under host load (load average 15–21), which matches a capture race rather than a deterministic incompatibility. Observed runs (same image, same args, 4x L20): | Run | Host load | Result | |---|---|---| | 2026-09-17 13:08 | idle | startup OK | | 2026-09-17 18:17 | load 15–21, 64-min slow weight load, `shm_broadcast` 60s stall warning beforehand | PIECEWISE 11/11 OK → FULL failed at 1/2, all 4 workers | | 2026-09-18 10:14 | moderate | startup OK | Full traceback (identical on all 4 TP workers): I could not attach `VLLM_TRACE_FUNCTION=1` logs for the failing run yet because the failure is intermittent and each reproduction costs ~1 hour of weight loading; happy to add them on the next recurrence. The crash is fully reproducible *in probability* under synthetic load (see below). The pinned-host PLE backend decorates `start_prefetch` with `eager_break_during_capture` (`vllm/models/qwen4_exp/nvidia/ngram_embedding.py`), launching the UVA lookup on a **side CUDA stream** and returning immediately. title: User-authored <|image_pad|> in text is misrecognized as image placeholder, causing image binding mismatch
body: vLLM’s generic multimodal `PromptReplacement` pipeline binds media items to placeholder occurrences after chat rendering and tokenization. The binding is based on token-value matching, not placeholder provenance. In the confirmed Qwen2.5-VL case, a literal `<|image_pad|>` in user text tokenizes to the same special-token id (`151655`) as the template-generated image placeholder. If the user-text occurrence appears first, it consumes the queued image update; the image feature span is inserted into user text, while the real `<|vision_start|><|image_pad|><|vision_end|>` image slot remains with one raw, unexpanded pad token. Token-level reproduction on the full chat path, using one 448x448 image (256 image tokens), gives: The layouts have the same length and token multiset; the processor trace shows that the media binding moved from the template-generated slot into user text. End-to-end tests on Qwen2.5-VL-3B and 7B then changed visual-safety verdicts from YES/UNSAFE to NO/SAFE and downstream decisions from BLOCK to ALLOW in the reported cells. A describe probe on the same allowed request still identified the depicted weapon, confirming that the image remained perceptible but was no longer structurally grounded at its intended slot. Component: vLLM multimodal prompt processing — generic `PromptReplacement` matching and placeholder validation. Files: Confirmed affected adapter: Source-level candidate adapters: The root cause is in vLLM’s generic multimodal prompt-update pipeline. Chat rendering produces a flat token sequence, and `PromptReplacement` later searches that sequence by token value. The pipeline does not retain whether a matched token originated from the chat template’s media placeholder or from user text. Therefore, any adapter that exposes a user-spellable placeholder string and uses token-value `PromptReplacement` can be susceptible. This report confirms the behavior on Qwen2.5-VL. Source references below are immutable links to the vLLM `v0.29.0` release tag
label: bug

title: `POST /reset_prefix_cache` returns success while the CPU offload tier keeps serving the same blocks
body: With a KV connector configured (`SimpleCPUOffloadConnector`), `POST /reset_prefix_cache` reports `{"success":true}` and clears the GPU prefix cache, but leaves the connector's CPU tier populated. The very next request for the same prompt is served from that tier: the GPU prefix-cache hit counter stays at zero while `vllm:external_prefix_cache_hits_total` jumps by the whole prompt. The endpoint's name and its success response suggest the engine is back to a cold prefix state. It is not, and nothing in the response or the logs says so. Any measurement that uses "reset, then send" as a cold baseline is silently measuring a warm path instead. Send a 1,024-token prompt, send it again, reset, send it a third time, then send it once more under a fresh `cache_salt`, reading `/metrics` between each step (`repro_reset_prefix_cache_offload_tier.py`, attached, is the same sequence in stdlib-only form and exits 1 when the tier serves the post-reset request). The reset does clear the GPU prefix cache: after it, `prefix_cache_hits_total` does not move. But `external_prefix_cache_hits_total` moves by 1,008 of the 1,024 prompt tokens, so the request was served from the CPU tier the reset left behind. Only a fresh `cache_salt` produces a genuinely cold path (last line: 1,024 external queries, zero hits). _Importance:_ Beyond the naming, the practical consequence is that "reset, then measure" is not a cold baseline on a connector arm, and there is no signal that it isn't. In our own testing this silently invalidated a four-way comparison: two byte-identical requests sent after a reset answered differently depending on which request had run *before* the reset, because each was served whatever the tier happened to hold. It took a dedicated probe to notice, because the endpoint reports success and the served-from-tier path is not visible in the response. _Expected behavior should prob be:_ One of: 1. `reset_prefix_cache` also drops the connector's cached blocks, or 2. it reports what it

title: Mamba-hybrid models cannot start with speculative decoding. Mamba page padding is planned without the speculative widening
body: Any Mamba-hybrid model whose `get_mamba_state_shape_from_config` does not pass `num_spec` fails to start when speculative decoding is enabled with `num_speculative_tokens >= 2`. The engine dies during startup with an `AssertionError` and no actionable message: Reproduce with the server: or offline, which is the smaller reproducer: `num_speculative_tokens=1` starts and generates correctly; `2` and above do not. Nothing about ngram is special, simply the method that needs no draft model. `repro_hybrid_spec_mamba_page_padding.py` (attached) is the offline form with `-k` and `--block-size` switches, so the three arms below (`-k 1` starts, `-k 2` asserts, `-k 2 --block-size 800` starts) are one script. The padded mamba page size is planned from a state shape that does not carry the speculative widening, while the layer's own state shape does. * `Platform.check_and_update_config` (`vllm/platforms/interface.py`) sizes `cache_config.mamba_page_size_padded` from `model_cls.get_mamba_state_shape_from_config(vllm_config)`. * For the affected models that classmethod calls `MambaStateShapeCalculator.mamba2_state_shape(...)` **without** `num_spec`, so the conv state is planned as `conv_kernel - 1` columns. * `MambaMixer2.get_state_shape()` (`vllm/model_executor/layers/mamba/mamba_mixer2.py`) passes `num_spec=self.num_spec`, so the real conv state is `conv_kernel - 1 + num_spec` columns. The real page is therefore wider than the planned one by `conv_dim * num_spec * itemsize`, and `MambaSpec.page_size_bytes` asserts. Whether it fires depends only on how much slack the padding happened to leave, which is why `num_speculative_tokens=1` slips through. On granite-4.0-h-tiny (bf16, TP=1): | | bytes | |---|---| | attention page (400 tokens × 2048 B) = planned padded mamba page | 819,200 | | mamba page at `num_spec=0` (conv 19,968 + ssm 786,432) | 806,400 | | incidental slack | 12,800 (1.59 %) | | added per speculative token (`conv_dim` 3,328 × 2 B) | 6,656 | | `num_spec=1` needs | 813,0

title: Mamba-hybrid models (granite-4.0-h) give a different, garbled greedy answer every time for a ONE-token prompt under full CUDA graphs
body: With **no flags** beyond `max_model_len`, a prompt that tokenizes to exactly one token is not deterministic at temperature 0, and most of its answers are unrelated to it. Prompts of two or more tokens are stable. You can use this for repro: [repro_hybrid_one_token_prompt_nondeterminism.py](https://gist.github.com/Yunzez/4a10e9529482318205b923613183327b#file-repro_hybrid_one_token_prompt_nondeterminism-py) Observed: Over the HTTP server (`vllm serve ibm-granite/granite-4.0-h-tiny --max-model-len 4096`, one request at a time, `temperature 0`, `top_p 1`, `top_k -1`, penalties neutral): **9 of 9** one-token prompts unstable (`Hello`, `Hi`, `Yes`, `No`, `Paris`, `Water`, `Once`, `The`, `2`; 4–6 distinct answers in 6 repeats each), **0 of 17** prompts of 2–6 tokens. Granite's tokenizer adds no BOS, techincally a one-token prompt is a prefill of exactly one token. Second hybrid family, same script: `tiiuae/Falcon-H1-Tiny-90M-Instruct`, **6 of 6** one-token prompts unstable (`Hello`, `Hi`, `Yes`, `No`, `The`, `2`; 5–6 distinct in 6), and every prompt of two or more tokens stable, including `Paris`, which is two tokens for that tokenizer. The boundary is the token count, not the word. | change | one-token prompts unstable | |---|---| | none (default) | 9 / 9 | | `--mamba-cache-mode align` | 9 / 9 (same) | | `--no-enable-prefix-caching` | still fails (`Hello` 4 distinct in 4) | | **`--compilation-config '{"cudagraph_mode":"PIECEWISE"}'`** | **0 / 40 prompts** | | **`--enforce-eager`** | **0 / 40 prompts** | Through the same offline script, `--piecewise` gives 0 of 11 prompts unstable. So it is the *full* CUDA-graph capture (the Mamba / attention kernels inside the graph) at the one-token prefill shape; the piecewise graph and eager mode are both correct and are the workarounds. Independent of the mamba cache mode and of prefix caching.

title: `prompt_embeds` + any penalty kills the engine with a device-side assert (`scatter gather kernel index out of bounds`)

title: --fingerprint-mode=none still emits "system_fingerprint": null in non-streaming responses
body: With `--fingerprint-mode=none`, the `system_fingerprint` value is correctly suppressed, but the key itself is still present in non-streaming `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/completions` responses, serialized as an explicit `null`: Response contains: Expected behavior: with `--fingerprint-mode=none`, the `system_fingerprint` key should be omitted entirely from the response body, matching what "the field is omitted" suggests in the `--fingerprint-mode` help text. Root cause: `none` mode makes `get_system_fingerprint()` return `None`, but non-streaming responses are serialized with `generator.model_dump()` in `vllm/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/api_router.py` without `exclude_none=True`, so the `None` value is emitted as an explicit JSON `null`. (Streaming paths use `exclude_unset=True`/`exclude_none=True` and are not affected.) This matters for clients doing strict schema conformance checks against the OpenAI spec, and for deployments that want minimal response surface. Note that unconditional omission would be a breaking change for the OpenAI Python SDK (`extra="allow"` turns absent keys into `AttributeError`), as discussed in #53349 — so any fix should either be opt-in (e.g. extending the approach of #53832 to cover `system_fingerprint`) or scoped to `none` mode only, where the user has explicitly asked for the field to be disabled.

title: TieringOffloadingSpec leaks /dev/shm mmap files on non-graceful shutdown (barrier-unlink fix from #52596 not applied)
body: PR #52596 fixed `SharedOffloadRegion` so the backing `/dev/shm/vllm_offload_{engine_id}.mmap` file is unlinked immediately after all workers have mapped it (via a `barrier` callback), so the kernel reclaims the memory on process exit regardless of how the process exits (including `SIGKILL` or a non-graceful container restart). However, this fix was only wired up in `vllm/v1/kv_offload/cpu/spec.py` (`CPUOffloadingSpec.create_worker`), which passes `barrier=_all_workers_barrier`. The `TieringOffloadingSpec` (`vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/spec.py`) creates **two** `SharedOffloadRegion` instances — the scheduler-side region (`get_manager`) and the worker-side region (`create_worker`) — **neither passes a `barrier`**. As a result, these regions still rely solely on the old `cleanup()`-on-graceful-shutdown path, and the `.mmap` file is leaked in `/dev/shm` whenever the engine process is killed non-gracefully (e.g. `SIGKILL`, OOM-kill, or a container restart that doesn't fully drain the graceful-shutdown signal chain). In a Kubernetes deployment using `medium: Memory` `emptyDir` for `/dev/shm` (shared at the Pod level, not the container level), restarting just the model container (without recreating the Pod) leaves the old engine's offload region file behind. The next engine startup generates a new `engine_id`/mmap file and needs the *full* configured offload size again, so `/dev/shm` free space is effectively halved (or exhausted) after every non-graceful restart, causing: RuntimeError: Insufficient space in /dev/shm: 131072 MiB required, 32768 MiB free. - `--kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"OffloadingConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_connector_extra_config":{"spec_name":"TieringOffloadingSpec","cpu_bytes_to_use":137438953472,"offload_prompt_only":false}}'` - Send `SIGKILL` (or `kill -9`) to the EngineCore process (or otherwise bypass the graceful shutdown path). - Observe `/dev/shm/vllm_offload_<old-engine-id>.mmap` still present after the process exits. - Restart the

title: nvidia/audio-flamingo-next-hf fails to load — get_audio_features() missing required argument 'input_ids'
body: `nvidia/audio-flamingo-next-hf` fails to load. vLLM resolves it to the Transformers backend, which then crashes during engine startup when it calls the model's audio encoder. Affects all three AF-Next checkpoints — `audio-flamingo-next-hf`, `audio-flamingo-next-think-hf`, `audio-flamingo-next-captioner-hf` (identical configs, different weights). HF's `MusicFlamingoModel.get_audio_features` takes `input_ids` as a required argument. It uses it to recover, for each 30-second audio chunk, that chunk's index within the audio it came from — which drives the model's rotary *time* embedding. vLLM encodes audio separately from the text tokens, so `_process_audio_input` has no `input_ids` to pass. This is not a tuning issue; the fallback is structurally unable to satisfy the signature. So the failure is on the vLLM side, not transformers. These checkpoints declare: vLLM had a `MusicFlamingoForConditionalGeneration` implementation through v0.24.0. It was removed in #47263, partly on the basis that *"MusicFlamingo has been superseded by AudioFlamingo3 (new MusicFlamingo checkpoints use AudioFlamingo3)"*. That does not hold for the Audio Flamingo Next family — all three variants declare `musicflamingo`, not `audioflamingo3`. The architecture is still listed in `_PREVIOUSLY_SUPPORTED_MODELS`, but that error path is never reached, since the Transformers fallback resolves first and fails as above. I have it working locally with token-level output parity against transformers and I plan to submit a PR.

title: assistant_tokens_mask misaligned after multimodal placeholder expansion
body: `assistant_tokens_mask` is built against the prompt before multimodal placeholders expand, and nothing expands the mask to match. Entry *i* stops describing token *i*, so a caller training on the mask scores the wrong tokens. `truncate_prompt_tokens` is not involved. transformers gets this right on the same input, so the divergence is vLLM's. Both produce 71 token ids; the masks differ. Reproduced on `main` at `dffbb714e`. No model weights, no GPU. The two APIs take audio differently, so the conversations differ only in how the same 4 seconds of silence is passed. Actual output: Expected: the mask has one entry per token, as transformers produces. vLLM's mask is short by 51, the 52-token audio span minus the single placeholder token it replaced. Every entry from offset 9 onward describes a token 51 positions earlier than the one it lands on. transformers tokenizes text and audio in one pass, so its mask covers the expanded audio. vLLM splits the two: `HfRenderer.render_messages` takes the mask from `apply_chat_template` against the unexpanded text (`hf.py:1109`), `_PARALLEL_TO_PROMPT_TOKENS` keeps it in step through tokenization, then `_process_multimodal` expands the placeholders and grows `prompt_token_ids` alone. `HfRenderer._process_tokens` attaches the unexpanded mask afterwards (`hf.py:1294`). Downstream, `scale_out/render/serving.py:129-148` pads the mask to length and logs "The mask may be positionally misaligned", which fixes the length and not the alignment. Stretching the mask after the fact does not look possible in the renderer: it needs to know how many original tokens each item consumed, and `mm_placeholders` records only where the content landed. `PromptReplacement` consumes its target sequence while `PromptInsertion` consumes nothing, so a 52-slot span could have come from one token, three, or none. title: Custom all-reduce start barrier is fully relaxed — peer-data reads unordered against remote (XGMI) writes → torn reads
body: - Upstream vLLM @ `241e9391ed85f6c967432135427717a529776a63` (2026-09-15), ROCm 7.0 clang for codegen evidence - 4× AMD Instinct MI100 (gfx908, XGMI full mesh), ROCm 7.14, torch 2.11.0+rocm7.1 On multi-GPU ROCm where P2P goes over XGMI (on 4× MI100 / gfx908, ROCm 7.14; where the memory-model argument applies wherever peers are remote agents relative to device scope), the custom all-reduce kernels can pass their start barrier and read a peer's staged input buffer while the peer's writes are still in flight. Torn bf16 values seed NaN/huge-finite activations; in-engine this presents as episodic single-layer corruption and, at long context, junk-token output walls. Load- and timing-dependent; silent. - `csrc/custom_collective_common.cuh` `barrier_at_start` (ROCm branch, lines 264–280): flag store to peers is `__ATOMIC_RELAXED` / `__MEMORY_SCOPE_SYSTEM`; flag load is `__ATOMIC_RELAXED` / `__MEMORY_SCOPE_DEVICE`. body: **My environment** - vLLM 0.27.1 (pip wheel), torch 2.13.0+cu130, RTX 4090 (sm_89); also reproduced on H100 (sm_90) with vLLM 0.25.1 and 0.27.1, and on A100-40GB (sm_80) with 0.27.1. - The kernel source is unchanged on `main` as of 2026-09-14 (`csrc/libtorch_stable/quantization/hadamard/hadacore/hadamard_transform_cuda.cu`, last touched by #42339). `torch.ops._C.hadacore_transform` returns wrong, run-to-run different values in the last `rows % 8` rows of its input whenever the input has more than 8192 rows and `rows % 8` is 1, 2, 3 or 4. Inputs with at most 8192 rows, or a remainder of 0, 5, 6 or 7, are correct. fp16 and bf16, d = 32 / 64 / 128 alike. repro: [repro_hadacore_tail_rows.py](https://gist.github.com/Yunzez/1f812fc3a124d71d744e00e3b153c370#file-repro_hadacore_tail_rows-py) **Mechanism** (read from the source, row rule and nondeterminism measured). The kernel works in warps of `num_chunks` 256-element chunks (two chunks of 8 rows at d = 64). The copy loop always issues and commits `num_chunks` `cp.async` groups per warp. When the padded chunk count is odd, the last warp owns a single real chunk (`real_num_chunks = 1`, `diff_num_chunks = -1`). In the masked wait loop the `cp.async.wait_group` is issued through `switch (k + diff_num_chunks)`, which for `k = 0` evaluates to `-1`; there is no such case, so no wait is issued and that warp reads its chunk from shared memory before the asynchronous copy has landed. With few blocks the copy usually wins; with a thousand or more blocks it frequently does not. A one-chunk tail is exactly `rows % 8 in 1..4`. What the warp reads is whatever the previous kernel left in that SM's shared memory. title: Qwen3-ASR audio preprocessing produces different audio-token counts from Hugging Face
body: Reproduced on unmodified upstream vLLM production code at commit: 000c7df9ffd3e470980fd4cd6b8ec1b0585500ff The source checkout lacks generated version metadata, so collect_env reports N/A (dev). This environment uses the checkout's Python source with existing vLLM 0.29 CUDA extensions, not a fresh CUDA build. Qwen3-ASR's vLLM audio processor produces different audio-placeholder counts from the checkpoint's native Hugging Face processor for the same waveform. For example, a 16,001-sample clip at 16 kHz produces 14 audio tokens in vLLM versus 13 in Hugging Face. This uses synthetic 16 kHz audio and does not load model weights. For each clip, vLLM should match the checkpoint's native HF preprocessing, including audio features and audio-placeholder counts. Two preprocessing differences appear responsible: - Qwen3-ASR inherits Omni's waveform padding to a multiple of the hop length, which can change feature lengths and audio-token counts. - Its processor hardcodes `WhisperFeatureExtractor` instead of honoring the native checkpoint's `Qwen3ASRFeatureExtractor`, including its minimum-length padding. I have a candidate fix and regression tests. Of 48 new cases, 34 fail on unmodified upstream; all 48 pass with the fix.

title: Humming MoE permute scratch memory scales with number of MoE layers
body: When using the Humming MoE backend, `MoEPermuteScratch` is currently owned by each `HummingExpertsBase` instance. For large MoE models, every MoE layer therefore keeps its own persistent permute scratch buffer, even though MoE layers execute sequentially and these buffers do not need to exist simultaneously. As a result, persistent GPU memory used by the Humming permute path scales with the number of MoE layers. Conceptually: The largest allocation in the scratch is the permuted hidden-state buffer, whose size scales approximately with: For models with many MoE layers, keeping one such buffer per layer can consume tens of GiB of persistent GPU memory. On GLM-5.3 NVFP4 with the Humming MoE backend, the layer-local scratch allocation caused a large persistent memory overhead. Before sharing the scratch workspace, the model could only start after reducing: After reusing a shared scratch workspace, the same TP=4 configuration can start with the default `max_num_batched_tokens`. The permute scratch should be treated as temporary execution workspace rather than layer-owned persistent state. Because MoE layers execute sequentially, compatible layers should reuse the same scratch allocation. For concurrent execution contexts, separate scratch buffers can still be kept per active `(ubatch, lane)` workspace to avoid aliasing. title: Triton attention softcap returns NaN for large attention logits
body: `apply_softcap` in `vllm/v1/attention/ops/triton_attention_helpers.py` computes `x * tanh(S / x)` as `x * (exp(S/x) - exp(-S/x)) / (exp(S/x) + exp(-S/x))`. Both exponentials overflow to `inf` when `|S / x| > ~88`, so the ratio is `inf / inf = NaN` and the whole attention row is poisoned. This path runs for models that use attention logit softcapping, for example Gemma-2 with `attn_logit_softcapping = 50`. A pre-softcap score above 4400 overflows. These models have very large attention logits, which is why they use softcapping. The same helper is used by the unified, DiffKV, and INT4 attention kernels. Reproduced on main at commit `c191787a68` with a GTX 1650 Ti and Triton 3.7.1. Reproduction: Observed: Expected: the softcap returns a finite value, `x * tanh(S / x)`, for every finite score. A stable form is `x * (1 - 2 / (exp(2 * S / x) + 1))`.
label: bug

title: Unconditional xgrammar import in backend_xgrammar.py crashes vLLM startup on s390x
body: On `s390x` (IBM Z / LinuxONE), vLLM 0.28.0 crashes at startup with an `ImportError` before serving any requests. The crash originates in `vllm/v1/structured_output/backend_xgrammar.py`, which imports `xgrammar` unconditionally at class-definition time. `xgrammar` has no pre-built wheels for `s390x` and cannot be built from source on the platform because it requires `apache-tvm-ffi`, which also has no `s390x` support. Because the import is unconditional and happens at module load, there is no way to use vLLM on `s390x` at all — including for workloads that never use structured output — without providing a stub module as a workaround. **Affected file**: `vllm/v1/structured_output/backend_xgrammar.py` **Proposed fix**: Wrap the import in a `try/except ImportError` guard, consistent with how other optional platform backends are handled throughout vLLM: Then raise a clear `RuntimeError("xgrammar is not available on this platform")` only if a user actually requests the xgrammar structured-output backend. **Current workaround**: Install a minimal Python stub package for `xgrammar` with a valid `__file__` attribute to satisfy the import. **Related**: #9652 — "[RFC]: Add support for IBM Spyre accelerator" — prior context for IBM Z / s390x vLLM support.
label: bug

title: JSON schema with multiple allOf branches is silently ignored by the xgrammar structured-output backend
body: A JSON schema that uses `allOf` with more than one branch is silently ignored by the default `auto` structured output backend. xgrammar 0.2.3 compiles a multi-branch `allOf` into a grammar that does not enforce the branches. The model can emit JSON that violates the schema, and vLLM reports no error. `auto` does not fall back to a backend that works, because the xgrammar feature gate `has_xgrammar_unsupported_json_features` does not list `allOf`. The `guidance` backend (llguidance 1.7.6) enforces the same schema correctly. Multi-branch `allOf` is common. Pydantic and OpenAPI emit it for model inheritance, for example `allOf: [{"$ref": "#/$defs/Base"}, {...}]`. The first row is valid. The next three violate `minimum: 10`, the `required` fields, or the object type, yet the grammar accepts all of them. In `auto` mode, vLLM enforces the schema, or rejects the request with a clear error. It must not return output that violates the schema without any signal. Start the server with `--structured-outputs-config.backend guidance`.
label: bug

title: /v1/messages non-streaming omits stop_sequence when null (exclude_none)
body: The non-streaming `/v1/messages` response has no `stop_sequence` key unless generation stopped on a matched stop string. `vllm/entrypoints/anthropic/api_router.py` serializes the response with `generator.model_dump(exclude_none=True)`, and `AnthropicMessagesResponse` declares `stop_sequence: str | None = None`, so the null value is dropped from the wire. `stop_reason` is dropped the same way when it is null. Anthropic's published schema lists both as required, nullable members of `Message` (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/messages, response fields `stop_reason` and `stop_sequence`; in the OpenAPI spec the SDKs are generated from, `Message.required` lists both and `stop_sequence` is `string | null`). Anthropic's own non-streaming examples carry `"stop_sequence": null`. The official SDKs tolerate the missing key; a schema-validating proxy does not, which is how this was found (vLLM Semantic Router, vllm-project/semantic-router#3500). This is the non-streaming twin of #55324. That one was `exclude_unset=True` on the streaming `message_delta`; this one is `exclude_none=True` on the buffered response, so the streaming fix does not cover it. `message_start` on the stream already carries both keys explicitly. Live, vLLM 0.26.0, `Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8`, `"stream": false`, content elided: Keys present: `content, id, model, role, stop_reason, type, usage`. No `stop_sequence`. Same on main at `828f4f19` (2026-09-10): `api_router.py` line 82. No GPU needed. Build the route's FastAPI app with a mocked handler that returns an `AnthropicMessagesResponse(stop_reason="end_turn")`, POST `/v1/messages` with `"stream": false`, and inspect `response.json()`: `"stop_sequence"` is not a key. Inspecting the model attribute hides the omission (`stop_sequence is None`); `model_dump(exclude_none=True)` reproduces it. With a server: `"stop_sequence": null` (and `"stop_reason": null` if ever null) on the non-streaming response, matching the schema and the streaming `message_delta` after

body: - vLLM main @ 7470082f5 (2026-09-10), Python sources with the v0.29.0 precompiled kernels (`VLLM_USE_PRECOMPILED=1`); also reproduced with the v0.29.0 wheel - torch 2.13.0+cu130, triton 3.7.1, NCCL 2.27.3 - 4x NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (sm_120, 96 GB), PCIe only (no NVLink), driver 580.159.04 - Model: `Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B` (bf16), attention backend `TRITON_ATTN` `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` is supposed to make outputs independent of the batch composition. title: Qwen3-VL fails when using modality-scoped image/video size kwargs (`images_kwargs` / `videos_kwargs`)
body: This appears to be a Qwen3-VL runtime regression/inconsistency related to the modality-scoped `mm_processor_kwargs` support introduced in #53808, which fixed #52834. A scoped partial `videos_kwargs.size` is resolved by vLLM and also materialized as a flat `size`, while the original nested `size` remains. Transformers therefore receives the same processor kwarg in both forms and rejects it as a duplicate. 2. Using a flat `size` instead made the override visible to vLLM, but also leaked it into the image budget. The Qwen3-VL runtime path currently violates that separation in the video case. title: Tool parser non-streaming parse drops post-tool-call text that streaming returns
body: For a model output that contains text before AND after a tool call, the two delivery modes disagree: streaming returns the post-tool text, non-streaming drops it. The tool parser is inconsistent with its own streaming mode. Reproduction (CPU only, no GPU or model weights; tokenizer download only): json\n" '{"city": "Paris"}\n Observed: The trailing "It is 30 degrees." is dropped by the non-streaming parse and kept by the streaming parse. Downstream, `messages_full_converter` (`/v1/messages` non-streaming) then never sees that text, while `message_stream_converter` emits it as a text block after the tool_use block - for the same generation, /v1/messages streaming shows the trailing text and non-streaming loses it. Non-streaming `extract_tool_calls` implementations truncate content at the tool-call start token and never resume afterwards: - deepseekv3_tool_parser.py: content = text before `<｜tool▁calls▁begin｜>` - hermes_tool_parser.py:109: `content = model_output[: model_output.find(self.tool_call_start_token)]` Streaming implementations emit post-tool text as content deltas (deepseekv3_tool_parser.py:248, `DeltaMessage(tool_calls=[], content=text)`). Both delivery modes return the same content for the same generation. Make the DeepSeek-V3 parser's non-streaming parse include the post-tool text, matching its own streaming mode. The same truncation exists in hermes_tool_parser.py and can follow separately if maintainers agree it is also unintended. OpenAI clients currently lose this text in non-streaming mode, so returning it is a correction, not a new feature.
label: bug

title: Beam Search ignores skip_special_tokens and exposes special tokens in decoded output
body: Online and offline Beam Search do not honor `skip_special_tokens` when constructing the final decoded text. This is especially visible with Voxtral Realtime transcription because the model intentionally generates control tokens such as `[STREAMING_PAD]` and `[STREAMING_WORD]` as part of its time-aligned decoding process. With regular sampling, these special tokens are filtered from the returned text. With Beam Search, they are exposed to the user, producing a response containing hundreds of internal control tokens. The generated token IDs are valid. The problem is limited to the final detokenization step. Mode | STREAMING_PAD | STREAMING_WORD -- | -- | -- Regular sampling | 0 | 0 Beam Search, n=2 | 185 | 27 The exact counts can vary, but Beam Search consistently exposes control tokens in the returned text. Beam Search should honor `skip_special_tokens`, consistently with regular sampling: - When `skip_special_tokens=True`, tokenizer-defined special tokens should be omitted from the returned text. - When `skip_special_tokens=False`, tokenizer-defined special tokens should be preserved. The final decoding performed by the online and offline Beam Search implementations calls tokenizer.decode(...) without forwarding skip_special_tokens. Additionally, the request's skip_special_tokens setting is not represented and propagated consistently through BeamSearchParams.
label: bug

title: mean_acceptance_length overcounts tokens when EOS occurs inside the accepted draft prefix
body: In vLLM v0.29.0, speculative decoding reports The documentation describes this quantity as: > Mean tokens emitted per verification step, including the bonus token. However, `accepted_draft_tokens + 1` is not always equal to the number of tokens actually emitted/committed by a verification step. In particular, this identity fails for the terminal verification step when an EOS token occurs inside the accepted draft prefix. For example, suppose a speculative verification step produces the following verified sequence: and all five draft tokens match the target model before stop handling. The current acceptance accounting records: and therefore this step contributes tokens to `mean_acceptance_length`. However, generation terminates at EOS, so the request actually commits only i.e. 3 tokens. The tokens after EOS are not emitted, and there is no emitted bonus token after EOS. More generally, if EOS is the `j`-th accepted draft token and the verifier reports `a >= j` accepted draft tokens, the current metric counts while the number of actually emitted tokens in that verification step is so the MAL numerator is overestimated by Even when EOS is the last accepted draft token (`a == j`), the metric is still overestimated by one because the bonus token is not actually emitted. This is not only a naming issue because `mean_acceptance_length` is commonly used to evaluate and compare speculative decoding methods. The current documentation defines it in terms of **emitted tokens per verification step**, but the implementation derives it from the number of accepted draft tokens plus an unconditional bonus token. Those quantities are equal for ordinary verification steps, but not for a terminal step that stops inside the accepted draft block. The same issue also affects the newly introduced per-request `mean_acceptance_length`, since `RequestSpecDecodeMetrics.to_dict()` computes from the acceptance histogram. title: --enable-lora + --enable-batch-sharded-sampling crashes at the first sampling step (no startup validation)
body: With `--enable-lora` and `--enable-batch-sharded-sampling` together, the engine starts cleanly and then the first request that reaches sampling fails with: Batch-sharded sampling exists to skip the TP logits gather: each rank computes partial-vocab logits and an all-to-all assembles full-vocab logits for rank-owned requests (`vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:1462` calls `model.compute_logits_local(...)` when a `BatchSharder` is active, created at `model_runner.py:439-451` whenever the model implements `compute_logits_local`). The lm_head LoRA delta can only be applied after that gather, so the LoRA logits processor rejects the skipped path outright (`vllm/lora/layers/logits_processor.py:158-165`): Every model that implements `compute_logits_local` passes `skip_gather=True`: `llama.py:557`, `qwen3_5.py:436`, `deepseek_v4/nvidia/model.py:1832`, `minimax_m3/nvidia/model.py`. With default LoRA targets, `lm_head` is wrapped (`vllm/lora/model_manager.py:499-525`), so the wrapped processor is what runs. `VllmConfig._validate_batch_sharded_sampling` (`vllm/config/vllm.py:2684`) already blocks `return_sampling_mask`, adaptive verification, `max_logprobs=-1` and `tp<=1` for the same reason, but has no LoRA blocker. The failing link executes on CPU (verified on main 58ad1f3b91, no GPU or model weights needed): Observed: Expected: the engine rejects the configuration at startup, the same way it already rejects `return_sampling_mask` or adaptive verification with batch-sharded sampling, instead of crashing per request at sampling time. `VllmConfig._validate_batch_sharded_sampling` should include a LoRA blocker so the combination fails fast at startup with a clear reason instead of a mid-serving `NotImplementedError`.

title: FixFunctionalizationPass crashes with "Tried to erase Node auto_functionalized but it still had N users" when the graph contains control_deps nodes
body: | | | |---|---| | vLLM | 0.28.0 | | PyTorch | 2.12.0 | | Python | 3.13.13 | | Platform | out-of-tree platform plugin (registered via the `vllm.platforms` plugin interface) | Compilation config in use when the crash occurs: In the failing graph, an `auto_functionalized` node handled by `FixFunctionalizationPass` still had a `control_deps` user when the pass attempted to erase it. Based on the code analysis above, a single such node appears sufficient to trigger the failure; multiple supported ops are not required. In our out-of-tree platform environment, this happened with a small **MoE** model. Three smaller / simpler models compiled successfully under the same configuration. We have not confirmed which graph-construction or scheduling step accounts for that difference, so this observation does not establish that the issue is specific to MoE models. The failure was observed on an out-of-tree platform backend. We have not verified the end-to-end MoE path on CUDA, and we have not obtained a working standalone reproducer in an upstream-only environment. title: Integrate CFT counted-write MoE all-to-all kernel
body: Integrate the CFT counted-write MoE all-to-all kernel introduced in [TensorRT-LLM PR #17647](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/pull/17647) into vLLM through FlashInfer. The kernel adds a Compute Fabric Transport (CFT) path for MoE dispatch and combine communication. It uses CUDA Logical Endpoints and `fabric.try_put.counted` operations to write directly into peer receive buffers over the NVLink fabric. A Logical Endpoint is a CUDA transport object representing a resource reachable over the NVLink fabric. Peers address its bound memory using an endpoint ID and offset rather than a mapped remote pointer. A counted write transfers data to a remote Logical Endpoint while atomically incrementing a destination-side counter by the number of bytes delivered. The receiver waits until the counter reaches the expected byte count before consuming the data. This combines data transfer and arrival notification to reduce nvlink latency, avoiding a separate fence-and-flag handshake between the sender and receiver. In throughput cases, because the counter adds to bytes transferred, it could lead to perf regressions. 1. @bobboli will first integrate the kernel into [FlashInfer](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer). 2. After the kernel is available through FlashInfer, vLLM should integrate it through the FlashInfer backend. 3. vLLM should detect the required capabilities at runtime and fall back to the existing MoE all-to-all path when they are unavailable. The TensorRT-LLM implementation requires CUDA 13.4+, `sm_100+` hardware, and a compatible NVLink fabric environment. - vLLM can use the CFT counted-write MoE all-to-all path through FlashInfer. - Unsupported or incorrectly configured systems automatically use the existing fallback. - Existing behavior remains unchanged unless the CFT path is explicitly selected or enabled by policy. - Heuristics determine when to enable counted writes based on workload characteristics. - Correctness tests cover both MoE dispatch and co

title: Lightweight vLLM Render API: Offload Heavy Multimodal Preprocessing from CPU Sidecars
body: Problem Statement In the current vLLM architecture, the render API (online_renderer.py -> renderer.render_chat_async -> _process_multimodal -> mm_processor.apply) handles everything from prompt template rendering to heavy multimodal processing. The execution pipeline currently performs the following steps inside apply(): | Step | What happens | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | Chat template | Messages rendered to a prompt string | Text only | | Media fetch + decode | URLs resolved, images/audio/video decoded | Network + CPU | | Item hashing | Per-item hash derived from the raw media, or a caller-supplied `uuid` | Keys the processor cache and the EC cache | | HF processor | Resize, normalize, patchify; produces `pixel_values`, `image_grid_thw`, … | The expensive step, Heavy CPU bound when having Multimodal Content | | Placeholder expansion | The single `<image>` token is replaced by N placeholder tokens | `_maybe_apply_prompt_updates` | | Placeholder extraction | `PlaceholderRange(offset, length, is_embed)` per item | Derived from the step above | While this works well for text-only workloads, running heavy Hugging Face processor pipelines (resizing, normalization, patchification, and tensor generation—especially for video and audio) inside the render API introduces severe CPU bottlenecks. Proposed Solution & Architecture 1. The vLLM render API should be lightweight and designed to run efficiently on lightweight CPU nodes. This is important for token-in/token-out 2. Lightweight MM Metadata Extraction (Ideal): Explore the feasibility of deriving token placeholder positions purely from media headers and dimensions (e.g., image/video resolution metadata) without executing the full HF image transformation pipeline. 3. GPU Offloading: Any heavy tensor-producing work (e.g., producing pixel_values) should be deferred or offloaded to the GPU worker pool in further phrases like encode stage rather than burdening the CPU-bound routing/rendering layer. _No response_ _No response_

title: Fast Start For vLLM
body: Fast Start reduces vLLM startup time by avoiding repeated checkpoint loading, weight processing, and kernel autotuning during engine restarts and scaling events. The core design uses a persistent per-GPU weight daemon. The daemon loads and processes model weights once, keeps sharded weights in GPU memory, and exposes them to new vLLM engines through CUDA IPC or a multi-node transport. When a compatible cache is unavailable, vLLM falls back to the existing checkpoint loader. - Reuse processed GPU weights across engine instances. - Support TP, PP, EP, multi-node deployments, and MTP. - Support quantized formats including FP8 and FP4. - Cache autotune results with hardware- and version-aware keys. - Preserve correctness through strict cache validation. - Provide a reliable fallback path for cache misses and failures. Cache entries are identified using model and checkpoint identity, quantization configuration, parallelism settings, GPU architecture, vLLM protocol version, and other relevant runtime metadata. Incompatible entries must never be silently reused. Cache misses, stale daemon connections, and validation failures produce diagnostics and fall back to the normal loading path when enabled. - lazy heavy imports (e.g. `torch._inductor`, which `vllm.env_override` imports eagerly); - no GPU queries at import time; - `fork` for workers when the parent has not initialized CUDA; - longer term, a warm "zygote" process kept by the daemon. - Daemon and engine in one container: CUDA IPC needs the same visible GPUs. - Persistent cache directories keyed by version. - The expected behavior for each failure mode. - Warm engine startup avoids repeated checkpoint loading. - Cached and regular loading produce equivalent model outputs. - Cache failures do not compromise correctness or availability. - Startup, cache-hit, fallback, transfer, and autotune timings are observable. _No response_ _No response_

title: KV cache events — bind-time ephemeral port allocation and a discovery API
body: Follow-up to #51275 (Race-free port management). KV cache events are currently classified there as "Category IV: static configured endpoints". This proposal applies the RFC's governing rule — *the process that binds chooses the port at bind time, and publishes the actual endpoint over an existing control path* — to the KV-events publisher, and adds the missing discovery path. Today a consumer of KV events across data-parallel ranks has no race-free way to know where each rank's publisher landed: - `KVEventsConfig.endpoint` requires an explicit port; the DP offset is arithmetic (`base_port + dp_rank`, `vllm/distributed/kv_events.py::offset_endpoint_port`). This is exactly the Category IV static formula: two deployments launched with the same base collide, and passing `tcp://*:0` degenerates to literal ports 0,1,2,... — rank ≥ 1 binds privileged/invalid ports. - `ZmqEventPublisher._socket_setup()` binds the socket but never reads back the assigned port (`zmq.LAST_ENDPOINT`), so with `:0` the OS-assigned port is silently discarded and `get_publisher_config()` still reports the pre-bind wildcard string. - `EngineCoreReadyResponse.kv_events_config` already carries the publisher config to the frontend, but `_apply_ready_response()` discards it; only the Rust gRPC `GetKvEventSources` consumes it, and it receives the unbound wildcard string. There is no Python/HTTP query surface. 1. **Bind-time allocation**: when the configured port is `0`, do not apply the DP offset — each rank's publisher binds `tcp://*:0` independently and the OS hands out distinct ephemeral ports. Explicit non-zero ports keep the existing `base + rank` behavior (backward compatible). 2. **Endpoint readback**: after `bind()`, read `zmq.LAST_ENDPOINT` (for pub and replay sockets), resolve `*` to a reachable host, and update `get_publisher_config()` to return the real bound endpoint. title: Add --gguf-dequant-on-load option to unlock cuBLAS tensor cores for prefill-heavy workloads`
body: `vllm_gguf_plugin` is popular for running quantized GGUF weights. During autoregressive decoding ($N=1$), memory bandwidth is the bottleneck, and on-the-fly dequantization (`ops.ggml_mul_mat_a8`) is fast. However, for prefill-heavy workloads (such as long-context prompts, batch embeddings, or dataset scoring on $T=8,192$), linear projections are **compute-bound**. On an RTX 4090 running Llama-3.1-8B-Q8_0 on an 8,192-token prompt: - `ggml_mul_mat_a8` takes **~18.2 ms per GEMM** ➔ **15.03 seconds** total model forward pass. - Native `bfloat16` cuBLAS tensor cores take **~1.7 ms per GEMM** ➔ **1.18 seconds** total model forward pass (**12.7x speedup**). Add an optional flag `VLLM_GGUF_DEQUANT_ON_LOAD=1` or `--gguf-dequant-on-load`. When set, the GGUF loader converts Q8_0 (or other compatible formats) to `torch.bfloat16` during model initialization: Users with enough VRAM to hold the unquantized weights (e.g. 16 GB for 8B on a 24 GB card) can immediately benefit from native cuBLAS tensor cores without having to convert GGUF files back to HuggingFace safetensors on disk. --- I searched out a bug and a couple performance optimizations while doing some research. I had the option of not doing anything, or having the LLM write the text. I hope that doesn't bother anyone. The bug was confirmed in another bug post, I added context / appended to the other bug report in terms of fixing it / root cause I determined. _No response_ Test environment as per collect_env

title: Zero-Copy In-Place KV-Cache Compactor via In-Situ Cycle Permutations (1.65x Speedup, 0 Bytes Aux VRAM)
body: In long-context LLM serving (32k to 128k+ tokens), dynamic KV-cache eviction/compaction algorithms (e.g., H2O, Scissorhands, StreamingLLM, or heavy-hitter pruning) are essential to prevent out-of-memory (OOM) faults. However, standard runtimes execute compaction using **out-of-place gathering** (`torch.gather` / dynamic tensor allocation): 1. **Auxiliary VRAM Spikes:** Allocating auxiliary buffers ($O(N \cdot D)$) triggers transient OOM faults during peak concurrency. 2. **HBM Memory Bus Saturation:** Double-buffering incurs redundant read/write transactions across the GPU memory bus. 3. **OS Allocation Latency Jitter:** Dynamic `cudaMalloc` calls introduce unpredictable serving latency spikes and degrade Time-To-First-Token (TTFT). We propose an in-situ idempotent permutation engine (`idempotent-kv`) implemented in OpenAI Triton that reorganizes multi-dimensional KV tensors **directly within existing HBM allocations** using **$O(1)$ scalar hardware registers**: - **Idempotent Invariant:** Enforces $f(f(x)) = f(x)$, locking retained active tokens into stabilized contiguous memory $[0, K-1]$. - **In-Register 2-Cycle Fast-Path:** Mutually transposed tokens are swapped directly within thread registers. - **Bitmask-Free Cycle Follower:** Detects cycle leaders on-the-fly via minimal index traversal, requiring 0 bytes of auxiliary index memory. - **100% Zero Auxiliary VRAM:** Exactly **0.00 MB** secondary global memory allocated. - **Bit-Exact Numerical Parity:** Zero approximation error ($\Delta = 0.000000$, 0 NaN). *Workload: Batch=1, Heads=32, SeqLen=8,192, HeadDim=128, Capacity=4,096 (50% Eviction, float16)* | Implementation | Latency (ms) | Peak Aux VRAM | VRAM Saved | Numerical Diff | | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | | **PyTorch Out-of-Place** | 3.350 ms | 96.00 MB | Baseline | Reference | | **`idempotent-kv` (In-Situ)** | **2.031 ms** | **0.00 MB** | **96.00 MB (100% Saved)** | **0.000000 (Bit-Exact)** | | **Improvement** | **1.65x Faster** | **0.00 MB** |

title: Validate hash-only decode requests in token-in/token-out protocol
body: The `token_in_token_out` `GenerateRequest` protocol currently accepts metadata-only multimodal requests (`features.kwargs_data is None`) with **no validation**. The generate worker silently constructs `mm_kwargs[modality] = [None] * len(hashes)` and forwards the request to the engine, which then fails downstream as an opaque `GenerationError` or `MultiModalCacheMissError` — depending on whether the item happens to be in the local cache. This is a correctness gap. A metadata-only request is legal in exactly two scenarios: 1. **Local cache hit** — the receiver's multimodal cache holds the items. A miss raises `MultiModalCacheMissError` (retryable, self-healing). 2. **Hash-only decode with remote prefill** — `kv_transfer_params` or `ec_transfer_params` signals that multimodal embeddings arrive out-of-band via the encoder-cache connector, so neither tensor data nor a local cache hit is expected. Without either transfer parameter, a metadata-only request is ambiguous: the generate worker has no way to resolve embeddings. Today it is accepted silently and fails late. **Proposed change:** add a `model_validator` on `GenerateRequest` that rejects `features.kwargs_data is None` when neither `kv_transfer_params` nor `ec_transfer_params` is set, with an actionable error message telling the caller exactly what to fix. This is a strict tightening — all currently-legal requests remain legal. The validator only catches requests that would have failed downstream anyway, but earlier and with a clear message. 1. **Do nothing (status quo).** Invalid requests fail as `MultiModalCacheMissError` or `GenerationError` deep in the engine. The error message does not mention `kv_transfer_params` or `ec_transfer_params`, so the caller has no way to know the fix. 2. **Validate in `serving.py` instead of the protocol.** Possible, but protocol-layer validation catches the error before any engine interaction and is testable without a running server. The validator is a focused protocol-layer guard

title: Restart Lifecycle Hooks for KV Transfer Connectors (NIXL)
body: Snapshot/Restore adapters generally require to dispose/reset/reinitialized on warm boot. KV-transfer connectors own transport resources that may need to be rebuilt during snapshot restore, device recovery, or planned transport restart. Currently the connector interface (`KVConnectorBase_V1`) has no way to drain transfers, release transport state, re-register existing KV caches, or verify readiness. We propose to add three connector lifecycle hooks: - `quiesce(timeout)` drains transfers and releases connector-owned transport resources while retaining KV-cache tensors; - `reinitialize()` creates fresh transport state and re-registers the retained caches; and - `verify()` validates local readiness before inference resumes. The base implementation is a no-op for compatibility. `MultiConnector` forwards the hooks to its configured children. NIXL implements the lifecycle, including rebuilding the state needed for peer handshakes. - Recreating the complete worker; but that would unnecessarily discard KV-cache tensors and unrelated worker state. - Adding NIXL-specific operations to the engine; it would couple the engine to one connector implementation. - We temporarily worked around the limitations by monkey-patching the engine, which is undesirable for obvious reasons This change defines the connector-side lifecycle boundary only. It does not define a snapshot format, external suspend/resume API, device recovery policy, or retry policy. The external lifecycle coordinator is responsible for serializing these calls and preventing new transfer work while quiescing. - NIXL pipeline-parallel support: #52913 - CUDA checkpoint/restore: #34303 - Container snapshot suspend/restore: #54940 - Restore implementation work: #54943 - llm-d snapshot orchestrator: llm-d/llm-d#2365 - NIXL stale-peer restart failure: #49238 - NIXL non-terminal transfer failure: #49528

title: Let `vllm launch render` / `--tokens-only` override an inherited `VLLM_ENABLE_SCALE_OUT_ENDPOINTS=0` instead of failing startup
body: Fail-closed is the right approach. A server that starts without any render routes would still pass its health check, only to return 404s for every request. That makes the problem much harder to diagnose. The problem is where the `0` comes from in practice. In llm-d / Dynamo-style deployments, `VLLM_ENABLE_SCALE_OUT_ENDPOINTS=0` is exactly the kind of value a platform or security team sets once as a cluster or namespace wide default. It could be a Helm global, a chart level `env` block or a namespace level pod default. That value is then inherited by every vLLM pod in the namespace including the render and `--tokens-only` pods and every one of them lands in `CrashLoopBackOff` at startup. Two things make this worse than a normal misconfiguration: 1. This unfortunately covers both halves of a disaggregated deployment. The check applies to `vllm launch render` and `vllm serve --tokens-only`, so a single inherited default takes down the renderer pods and the token-in/token-out engine pods together. 2. The person who sets the default is usually not the person who writes the pod spec. A platform team hardening a namespace has no reason to know that two specific launch commands treat the variable as fatal rather than as a default. The current guidance is to "unset it or set it to 1" but unsetting is not available in the configurations above. You cannot remove an env var injected by a namespace default or a Helm global from a downstream pod spec. You can only override it with another value. So the only workable remedy today is "every render and `--tokens-only` pod must set `VLLM_ENABLE_SCALE_OUT_ENDPOINTS=1` explicitly" and that requirement is not stated anywhere. There is also a precedence question worth settling on its own merits. `vllm launch render` is a command explicitly for disaggregated deployment. The env var should not affect this command. Make the explicit launch mode always start: - `vllm launch render` and `vllm serve --tokens-only` register their required endpo
label: feature request

title: Support Sentence Transformers Transformer-Pooling-Dense CrossEncoders
body: Sentence Transformers can save CrossEncoders as explicit module chains. The standard layouts include: - `Transformer` for sequence classification - `Transformer → LogitScore` for causal-LM rerankers - `Transformer → Pooling → Dense` for a feature-extraction backbone with a trained scoring head The first layout already maps to vLLM's sequence-classification path, and vLLM has model-specific support for some causal-LM rerankers. The remaining gap is that vLLM does not interpret the saved Sentence Transformers module stack and its configs. An immediate use case is a multimodal cross-encoder reranker saved as `Transformer → Pooling → Dense`. The Dense layer contains trained checkpoint weights, while the Pooling and Transformer configs define how hidden states and structured multimodal pairs are processed. Sentence Transformers can reload the complete model, but vLLM currently cannot discover the scoring head or reproduce those saved semantics without model-specific code or launch-time overrides. This issue proposes bounded support for the standard serialized layout, starting with the exact `Transformer → Pooling → Dense` chain: - read the CrossEncoder and module metadata saved with the checkpoint - map supported pooling modes to vLLM's pooling runner - load the trained Dense scoring head and its activation - preserve supported structured multimodal input formatting - fail clearly when the checkpoint uses unsupported modules or semantics - leave non-pooled CrossEncoders on their existing vLLM paths This would let the same checkpoint load in Sentence Transformers and vLLM without `trust_remote_code` or a model-specific vLLM implementation. - Add a model-specific sequence-classification implementation in Transformers. This makes the checkpoint portable to Transformers, but fixes the pooling and scoring design at the model-class boundary and requires upstream support for each model family. - Add another model-specific reranker path in vLLM. title: Tokenized Prompt as Input for Chat and Messages Endpoints when serving
body: It would be useful for vLLM HTTP serving endpoints such as `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/messages` to accept prompt token IDs as input and skip repeated tokenization, while still preserving normal handling for tools, reasoning, and multimodal content. The concrete examples below focus on `/v1/chat/completions`, but the same need also applies to agent-style message APIs. This is related to the earlier feature request in [vLLM issue #25051](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/25051) (Stale, closed, and maybe outdated). The main goal is simple: if a frontend already has prompt token IDs, vLLM's HTTP chat/message endpoint should be able to consume those IDs directly and skip tokenization. For example, an HTTP routing layer such as vLLM Router may tokenize requests before forwarding them to workers so it can reuse repeated prompt prefixes, estimate prefill cost, or make cache-aware scheduling decisions. If `/v1/chat/completions` cannot accept those token IDs, vLLM has to apply the chat template and tokenize again. Current flow: Desired flow: For pure completion-style requests, vLLM already supports this pattern. `/v1/completions` can accept token IDs through the `prompt` field: Offline and lower-level generation paths also support token-ID-style inputs. Internally, tokenized multimodal inputs are represented as token IDs plus separate multimodal payload fields, not as token IDs alone. For chat-style endpoints, however, users currently cannot cleanly provide the already-tokenized chat prompt through the OpenAI-compatible HTTP API. This blocks tokenization-cache reuse at the HTTP frontend layer and can cause duplicate work: 1. A frontend applies the chat template and tokenizes the prompt for tokenization-cache reuse or scheduling/cache logic. 2. vLLM receives the original chat request and applies the chat template/tokenizes again. title: Add explicit cache IDs for reusable multimodal and inference state
body: There are already several caching mechanisms in vLLM, including multimodal processing/encoder caching and prefix caching. It would be useful to expose an explicit, application-level cache_id (or similar handle) for reusable cached state. The idea is simple: an application sends a large context or image once, vLLM performs the expensive processing and returns a cache_id. Subsequent requests could reference that ID instead of sending and processing the same data again. For example: large document / image ↓ process once ↓ cache_id ↓ question 1 question 2 question 3 ... The handle would be implementation-independent: it could refer to multimodal/vision state, prefix/KV state, or other expensive intermediate state. This would be particularly useful for workloads where the same document or image is queried many times, such as RAG, document analysis, multimodal agents, and batch processing. The main goal is to let applications explicitly retain and reuse expensive computation, rather than relying only on automatic cache matching. The existing automatic prefix caching and multimodal UUID mechanisms are useful, but they still require the application to work with the specific caching mechanism. An explicit cache_id would provide a simple, unified application-level handle while allowing vLLM to decide internally what representation is stored and how it is managed. _No response_

title: Entropy-Gated Dynamic Speculative Decoding (Dynamic k in {0, K}) via Real-Time Shannon Hysteresis
body: Standard speculative decoding in vLLM operates with a static draft length ($k = \text{constant}$). However, during high-entropy generation steps (e.g., complex reasoning forks, multi-lingual syntax, or high-perplexity code tokens), the token acceptance rate $\beta \to 0$. This leads to frequent draft rejection rollbacks, net throughput degradation ($S < 1$), and wasted compute FLOPs/energy. We propose an **Entropy-Gated Stochastic Speculative Controller** that evaluates output distribution Shannon entropy $H(t)$ in real-time and dynamically modulates the draft window: - **$k = K$ (e.g., 5)** during low-entropy deterministic spans (~100% draft acceptance). - **$k = 0$ (single-step fallback)** during high-entropy cognitive search forks, completely eliminating wasted draft passes. To prevent rapid mode-thrashing (gear hunting) on borderline tokens, the controller uses an industrial **Schmitt-trigger hysteresis loop** with EMA smoothing ($\alpha = 0.35$). --- 1. **Numerically Stable Float32 Shannon Entropy:** $$\log p_i = \text{LogSoftmax}(z_i) = z_i - \log \sum_{j \in \mathcal{V}} e^{z_j}$$ $$H(X) = - \frac{1}{\ln 2} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{V}} e^{\log p_i} \cdot \log p_i$$ 2. **Hysteresis State Transitions:** $$ \bar{H}_t = \alpha \cdot H(p_t) + (1 - \alpha) \cdot \bar{H}_{t-1} $$ $$ k_t = \begin{cases} 0, & \text{if } S_{t-1} = \text{Active} \land \bar{H}_t > \theta_{\text{high}} \\ K, & \text{if } S_{t-1} = \text{Fallback} \land \bar{H}_t < \theta_{\text{low}} \\ k_{t-1}, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$ *(Default baseline thresholds: θ_low = 0.55 bits, θ_high = 1.25 bits).* --- We benchmarked this control mechanism on Llama-3.1-8B under 100 Hz NVML hardware power polling: - **Electrical Energy per Token:** Reduced by **46.7%** ($6.40\text{ J} \to 3.41\text{ J/token}$). - **Throughput:** Maintained **50.52 tok/s** on complex poetic generation (409 generation steps). - **Draft Rejection Waste:** The clutch successfully locked at $k=5$ for 150+ continuous steps during d

title: Per-request and per-session KV cache tier attribution in OpenTelemetry traces
body: When running hierarchical KV cache tiering (GPU -> CPU -> filesystem via `TieringOffloadingSpec`), operators have no way to trace a single request or session and see which tier served its cached blocks or how long promotion took. The existing `llm_request` OTel span only includes latency and token count attributes. Aggregate per-tier Prometheus metrics exist (`block_hits`, `block_queries`, `read_time` by tier label), but they cannot answer: "Did this specific slow request hit the filesystem tier, and how long did promotion take?" or "How are tier hits distributed across requests in this agentic session?" **Proposal:** Add per-request KV cache tier attribution as span attributes on the existing `llm_request` OTel span. When tiering is enabled and tracing is active, the span would include attributes such as: - `kv_cache.request_id` : the request ID - `kv_cache.session_id` : the session ID, if set (already available on requests via #48048) - `kv_cache.tier_hit` : which tier(s) served cached blocks (e.g., `cpu`, `fs`, `none`) - `kv_cache.blocks_hit` : number of blocks served from cache, by tier - `kv_cache.blocks_missed` : number of blocks that required recomputation - `kv_cache.promotion_latency_seconds` : total promotion time from secondary tier to primary, if applicable Including `session_id` enables operators to filter traces by session, making this useful for agentic workloads where multiple requests share KV cache state within a conversation. This aligns with the session-centric KV cache orchestration direction proposed in RFC #48501. `TieringMetricsTracker` already tracks per-request lookup state internally (`_request_states` dict keyed by `req_id`), including which tier each block resolved at. However, this data is aggregated into counters and the per-request identity is lost at stats collection time. The implementation would extend this existing state to surface a per-request summary through the stats pipeline into the OTel span. - **Structured logging**: Emit
label: feature request

title: Support auxiliary-GPU offloading for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next N-gram / PLE embeddings
body: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next introduces a very large N-gram / PLE embedding table. title: Rust frontend: /v1/embeddings endpoint
body: Right now, with VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND=1, hitting /v1/embeddings just returns a 404 Not Found. For example, a simple curl like this: gets back a `404` with an empty body. So the endpoint simply isn't there – you can't use embeddings at all with the Rust frontend enabled, and you're forced to fall back to the Python version. That's the pain point this PR fixes. We're adding `/v1/embeddings` support to the Rust frontend. It handles text and token inputs, batched requests, float/base64 encoding, the dimensions param, LoRA adapters, and usage reporting – fully OpenAI-compatible. Right now the Rust frontend doesn't support embeddings, but a lot of common use cases (RAG, semantic search, classification) need it. If you enable the Rust frontend with VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND=1, you can't use embeddings and have to switch back to the Python frontend – which is a pain. Adding this endpoint makes the Rust frontend actually usable for embedding workloads. This is explicitly listed in the Rust frontend feature parity roadmap (#44280) under "Pooling / embedding APIs". We already have PR #53736 ready. Once merged, we're one step closer to making the Rust frontend the default option. We already have PR https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53736 ready
label: feature request

title: Enable varlen for GLM-5.x/DSV3.2 (Sparse MLA)
body: Adaptive verification has a firm requirement that the attention backend must not use the CPU-side query lengths as a source-of-truth, instead using the GPU tensors (so that we can run the confidence-based assignment on the GPU without synchronizing the CPU). Additionally, kernels must be able to support decode batches where requests have different query lengths per request. GLM-5.x models using DSV3.2-style sparse MLA should be compatible through FlashInfer's SM100 TRT-LLM sparse-MLA kernel. vLLM currently derives the sparse token-to-request mapping from CPU query boundaries, and the target capability check also includes draft attention that is captured by a separate graph manager. We should wire up the device-length path, validate correctness, evaluate performance, and merge support. PROPOSED IN https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52783 DEPENDS ON https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/47808 Parent tracker: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/51303

title: Support per-request dynamic LoRA scale
body: Currently `LoRARequest.lora_scale` is fixed at request creation and baked into the CUDA graph / kernel as a scalar. This prevents: - same-adapter requests in one batch from using different strengths; - adjusting LoRA strength mid-generation. A real ASR service works around this by baking scale into separate adapter copies (one slot per scale). This wastes slots and limits scale to discrete presets. **Proposal:** Add `LoRAScaleState` — a per-request `UvaBackedTensor` (`[max_num_reqs]`) following `SamplingStates`, passed to the LoRA kernel along with `token_to_req`. Effective scale = `base_scale * request_lora_scales[token_to_req[token_idx]]`. No per-token memory, CUDA-graph-compatible. **Evaluation (real adapter + WER A/B):** | Condition | CN mean \|B-A\| | EN mean \|B-A\| | | --- | --- | --- | | off (noise floor) | 0.022% | — | | 1.0 pre-fix | 17.184% | — | | 1.0 post-fix | 0.038% | 0.028% | - 4 adapter slots → 1 slot. - Arbitrary continuous scale values. - Two bugs found & fixed: CUDA graph captured the scale-free kernel variant (`tl.constexpr`), and the all-ones buffer wasn't refreshed. - **Baking scale into separate adapter copies** (current workaround) — consumes one adapter slot per scale, limited to discrete presets such as `LORA_SCALES=0.5,0.7,0.9,1.0`. - **Storing a per-token scale array** — would require more GPU memory (e.g. 128 KB per batch vs 1 KB per request) and does not follow vLLM V1 persistent-batch style. - Full per-test-set breakdowns and logs are available on request. - Happy to open a PR if this direction is reasonable.
label: feature request

title: Low-overhead asynchronous early-exit checks & KV-cache reclamation for Continuous Batching
body: Problem Statement In high-throughput production environments running long-context agent loops or strict JSON-enforcement pipelines, models frequently burn a significant portion of generation cycles on post-plateau tail-tokens (e.g., polite wrappers, redundant formatting) after the core semantic task is complete. While stop_strings and custom LogitsProcessor hooks exist, evaluating them per-step in Python introduces severe bottlenecks: CPU-GPU Sync & GIL Contenter: Per-step synchronous callbacks disrupt the execution loop, create heavy interpreter friction, and degrade throughput at scale (batch size > 64). Even in Python-heavy orchestration stacks, this creates unacceptable micro-lags. KV-Cache Bloat & Fragmentation: Finished or logically complete sequences linger in the active batch until the explicit stop token hits or max tokens are reached, occupying precious blocks in PagedAttention and artificially inflating latency for concurrent requests. An Economic Perspective In high-volume enterprise deployments (e.g., fintech, customer ops, logistics), long-context generation loops routinely burn 20–30% of output tokens on post-plateau tail generation. For enterprise clients processing tens of millions of requests monthly, this translates to hundreds of thousands of dollars in wasted infrastructure costs annually, plus artificial latency inflation due to occupied KV-cache slots. Has anyone in the community tackled token overconsumption and mid-batch memory reclamation from a production-economy standpoint? How are large-scale deployments justifying or mitigating these dead compute cycles today? Proposed Solution Introduce a lightweight, optimized mechanism at the scheduler level to handle dynamic early-exit flags and asynchronous KV-cache recycling without heavy interpreter roundtrips: Allow registering low-overhead termination predicates directly within the vLLM scheduler loop. title: Refactor EPD
body: vLLM has the EPD scaffolding (`vllm/distributed/ec_transfer/`, `ECConnectorBase` with scheduler + worker roles, `ECConnectorFactory`, `ec_transfer_params` in the OpenAI layer, E→PD / E→P→D examples). But **every existing EC connector transfers synchronously and locally**, and the encode → stage → send → release flow is hard-wired to that assumption: - `ECExampleConnector` — `save_caches()` writes a safetensors file to shared disk; the consumer `start_load_caches()` reads it back. Blocking, filesystem-bound. - `ECCPUConnector` — offloads the encoder cache into a CPU mmap region on the same host. Blocking, single-host only. There is **no over-the-wire backend**: the encoder and PD instances must share a filesystem or a host. By contrast the KV path already ships pluggable network transports (`NixlConnector`, `MooncakeConnector`, … in `vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/factory.py`). The EC path needs the same: a refactor that turns the single hard-coded transfer path into a **backend-agnostic pipeline** where new transports plug in cleanly. The core goal is the **refactor** — make the encoder-instance flow backend-agnostic so that supporting many transfer backends is a matter of implementing a delivery interface, not rewriting the pipeline. The first two backends to land on top of it: 1. **`ECZmqConnector`** — producer pushes the embedding over a ZMQ socket to the consumer (PD scheduler). Simple, dependency-light, works across nodes. 2. **`ECMooncakeConnector`** — RDMA transfer: the consumer registers a landing buffer and reads the embedding out of the producer's GPU buffer. High throughput for large embeddings. These backends are **asynchronous** and **cross-process**, which the current blocking `save_caches` / `start_load_caches` contract cannot express safely. The refactor exists precisely to make async, over-the-wire transfer correct — and to make the *next* backend after these two trivial to add. Everything after `receive` should follow a single chain, so

title: split local/external prefix-cache hits in `prompt_tokens_details`
body: With distributed prefix caching (KV connectors such as Mooncake / lmcache), cache hits in a single prefill can come from two different sources: - **local**: hits on this instance's GPU prefix cache; - **external**: hits fetched from a remote KV store / another instance via the KV connector. The scheduler already tracks `num_local_cached_tokens` / `num_external_cached_tokens` separately in `PrefillStats`, but `OutputProcessor` only forwards their sum (`num_cached_tokens`), so the breakdown is lost before it reaches the OpenAI serving layer — users cannot tell, per request, where cache hits came from. Exposing this information per-request may also be handy for pricing purposes. With `--enable-prompt-tokens-details` enabled, the response currently looks like: Add two optional keys, `local_cached_tokens` / `external_cached_tokens`, alongside the existing fields: Invariant: `cached_tokens == local_cached_tokens + external_cached_tokens`. - Strictly additive change: existing fields (`cached_tokens` / `created_cache_tokens` / `multimodal_tokens`) must be preserved untouched; - New fields default to `None` and must not affect existing output when the flag is off or the values carry no meaning; - Cover both streaming and non-streaming paths for chat and completion endpoints, and also benefit offline `LLM()` users. _No response_ _No response_

title: Parse Request Priority from HTTP Header
body: As part of company ops, being able to adjust the request priority at an intermediate proxy/load balancer by changing/setting a HTTP header makes it an order of magnitude easier than having to use more specialized tooling to parse the entire request and modify JSON structure. Suggestion: `X-Vllm-Priority` Priority from a header must override any priority found in the request body. The information about the intended priority of requests is often neither of concern, nor even available to individual clients where requests originate. Priority could also change arbitrarily due to ops requirements or business decisions, potentially affecting many clients, which would all have to be reconfigured/reloaded in their own way. A workaround would be having a more complex proxy that is specific to LLM APIs and implements this adjustment or generic enough to offer facilities for manipulating requests. It would need to wait for the entire JSON request, set the field and then pass the request on. For processing of large chats or especially attached files/images, requests can become large, resulting in a lot of overhead and delay on any proxy. _No response_

title: Emit BlockInactive KV events when GPU block ref_cnt drops to zero
body: Add a new KV cache event type, `BlockInactive`, published when a GPU prefix-cached block's `ref_cnt` drops from 1 to 0 in `BlockPool.free_blocks()`. This is distinct from existing events: - `BlockStored`: block becomes actively referenced / stored - `BlockRemoved`: block is physically evicted from memory - `BlockInactive` (proposed): block still resides in GPU memory, but no request currently references it In PD-disaggregated serving, an external scheduler (e.g. a KV-aware router / load balancer) may track per-decode-worker active KV occupancy for decode-node selection, for example: load_score = (query_block_len - overlap_depth) + active_blocks Today, consumers can observe BlockStored / BlockRemoved, but they cannot reliably detect that the last request released a block while it may still sit in the prefix cache. Without a refcount-zero signal, active_blocks tends to only increase, or requires fragile heuristics. I'm working on decode-affinity routing for PD clusters and need a clean, engine-native signal for "GPU block is no longer actively referenced." In BlockPool.free_blocks(), when ref_cnt == 0, enable_kv_cache_events is on, and the block has a hash, append BlockInactive(block_hashes=..., medium=MEDIUM_GPU). Publish via the existing KV event path (ZMQ / take_events()). No new scheduler-loop wiring. Role gate: Prefill-only instances (kv_role == "kv_producer") still emit BlockStored / BlockRemoved, but do not emit BlockInactive, so Prefill frees do not pollute decode load signals. Decode (kv_consumer), union (kv_both), and non-PD setups continue to emit Inactive. Gate with kv_role != "kv_producer" (do not use is_kv_producer, which includes kv_both). Rough mapping to ref_cnt: 0 -> 1 BlockStored N -> N+/-1 (>0) (no new event) 1 -> 0 BlockInactive (proposed) eviction BlockRemoved (unchanged) I have a draft implementation on a fork and can open a PR after discussion. It adds BlockInactive in kv_events.py, gates emission via KVTransferConfig.should_emit_block_inactive

title: Expose startup status and health endpoint before model engine is ready
body: vLLM currently exposes its HTTP API only after the model engine has completed initialization. For models with expensive startup phases, this can leave the service unreachable for a long time even though the process is alive and making progress. For example, startup may include: Loading model checkpoints Compiling execution paths Allocating KV cache FlashInfer or backend autotuning CUDA graph capture Model-specific kernel warmup With large or hybrid models, these phases can take many minutes. During that period, an external orchestrator or monitoring system cannot distinguish between: Normal initialization A stalled startup An out-of-memory condition A crashed worker A restart loop A process that is alive but not yet ready to serve inference I would like vLLM to expose a lightweight management or health endpoint before the model engine is ready. A possible design would separate process liveness, startup state, and inference readiness: Example startup response: A minimal implementation does not need an estimated completion time or exact percentage. Even a stable state and phase enum would be useful: The management endpoint should be served by a lightweight component that starts before engine initialization and remains available if model initialization fails. This would make vLLM much easier to operate behind Kubernetes, systemd, appliance supervisors, load balancers, and enterprise monitoring systems. The goal is not necessarily to reduce startup time.
