This is required for the vision `mm_prefix` / PrefixLM bidirectional mask path, and avoids mixing FlashAttention and Triton attention implementations within the same model. For video prompts, however, the current FA4 `mm_prefix` implementation scales poorly when the number of multimodal ranges varies across requests and batches. In Gemma4 video workloads each frame commonly contributes one range, so batches may see `max_ranges` values such as 1, 8, 16, 32, 46, or 64 over time. This is not limited to applications that pre-extract frames outside vLLM. The native vLLM video ingestion path can also produce variable frame counts. title: Add DFly speculative decoding and D-Cut support
body: We would like to propose adding DFly speculative decoding support to vLLM, together with D-Cut, a dynamic draft pruning method for speculative decoding. DFly is the main speculative decoding method in this proposal. Existing DFlash/DSpark-style paths are treated as baselines or compatibility foundations. The primary goal is to make DFly usable in vLLM's standard serving stack and improve its runtime efficiency with D-Cut. This proposal focuses on two main features: DFly is a speculative decoding method that uses a draft model to generate candidate tokens for the target model to verify. The proposed integration adds support for running DFly-style draft models inside vLLM, including: - recognizing DFly draft model architectures - registering the DFly draft model implementation - routing DFly through the speculative decoding runtime - supporting the required draft-token transport and verification flow - keeping compatibility with existing speculative decoding infrastructure The expected result is that users can serve target models with a DFly draft model through normal vLLM APIs, without relying on an external or out-of-tree runtime. D-Cut is a dynamic pruning strategy for speculative decoding. Instead of always verifying a fixed number of draft tokens, D-Cut chooses how many draft tokens to keep for each request based on draft confidence and runtime cost. This helps avoid wasting verification compute on low-confidence draft tokens. At a high level, D-Cut provides: - per-request dynamic keep-length selection - confidence-based draft pruning - scheduler-side truncation of draft tokens - keep-ratio metrics - optional cost-aware automatic mode - integration with the DFly speculative decoding path D-Cut is intended to improve the efficiency of DFly by adapting the verification width to each request. Speculative decoding performance depends heavily on both draft quality and verification cost. A fixed draft length can be suboptimal: - if the draft model is confident, verifyi

title: Balanced MoE routing between GPUs
body: With expert parallelism each EP rank owns an equal number of experts. As tokens get routed to the experts, the MoE computations are bottlenecked by the rank that receives the most tokens. I developed a patch that routes tokens to the experts in a balanced way so that each GPU rank gets approximately equal number of tokens. This increases performance significantly (see the benchmark table below). As a result, a given token might not always get the best possible expert, but rather it gets routed to the best available (under loaded) expert. This might affect the accuracy slightly, but we can adjust the intensity of the feature by a "capacity_factor" that enables us to control the tradeoff between performance and accuracy. In the future we could also introduce redundant experts that may allow us to eliminate the accuracy regression completely. Vllm benchmark validation: Image: vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:v0.25.1 Model: deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3 ISL: 4096 OSL: 256 max_concurrency: 128 | MOE_balancing | Capacity_factor | Requests/s | Tokens/s | TTFT | TPOT | gsm8k accuracy| |---------------|-----------------|-----|----------|------|------|-------| | Off | inf | 3.23 | 14060 | 1780 | 143 | 95.07 | | On | 1.5 | 3.38 | 14712 | 1678 | 137 | 94.84 | | On | 1.2 | 3.46 | 15036 | 1629 | 134 | 93.33 | All comments and ideas regarding this topic are welcome. We were also looking into the Expert Parallelism Load Balancer (EPLB) that was developed in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/18343. However, this feature didn't provide any uplift for our workload, and it was also incompatible with VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_FUSION_SHARED_EXPERTS. title: w8a8_block_int8_matmul kernel is dormant
body: `w8a8_block_int8_matmul` still exists in `vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/utils/int8_utils.py`, but there is no in-tree production dispatch to it in current vLLM main. The former wrapper, `apply_w8a8_block_int8_linear`, was later removed in PR #47329 as unused dead code. The key distinction is that the kernel landed, but the upstream quantization-method integration did not. In contrast, the block-FP8 path is documented and actively supported in vLLM, while current vLLM INT8 support is documented through other W8A8 flows rather than this block-INT8. - PR #13942 was the upstream attempt to add a full `blockwise_int8` integration, including config and dispatch for models such as `meituan/DeepSeek-R1-Block-INT8`, but it never landed. Issue #14176 was a separate request for DeepSeek-R1 block/channel INT8 support and likewise did not produce merged upstream support. - PR #16366 added the Triton-side block-INT8 kernel scaffolding, including `w8a8_block_int8_matmul`, but not a lasting upstream serve path.PR #47329 later removed `apply_w8a8_block_int8_linear`, which is consistent with the absence of any surviving upstream caller. The most accurate current description is: upstream vLLM still contains the block-INT8 GEMM kernel implementation, but not an upstream quantization config or linear-method path that would select it during normal serving. So the code is present but unreachable from mainline model dispatch. Separately, the published vLLM docs show active support for FP8 and other INT8/W8A8 quantization workflows, which should not be conflated with this specific block-INT8 path. vLLM's `_w8a8_block_int8_matmul` body is structurally identical to sglang's `python/sglang/kernels/ops/quantization/int8_kernel.py::_w8a8_block_int8_matmul` Filing to document the state and surface the decision that hasn't been made anywhere in-tree, so it's discoverable next time someonenruns into the gap. title: Integration of HieraSparse N:M Semi-Structured Sparse KV Cache Attention
body: As context lengths scale to 64k–192k+ tokens, TTFT (Time-To-First-Token) and memory footprint become significant bottlenecks in long-context LLM serving. While unstructured pruning drops elements without offering compute speedup, and coarse-grained token/head pruning can degrade model accuracy, modern NVIDIA GPUs (Ampere, Hopper) feature **2:4 N:M sparse tensor cores** that offer up to 2× speedup for sparse GEMMs. Currently, vLLM lacks native support for semi-structured N:M sparse KV cache acceleration using hardware sparse tensor cores. --- We request native integration or an experimental backend feature based on the [HieraSparse architecture](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.16864) ([GitHub Repo](https://github.com/psl-ntu/HieraSparse)). HieraSparse introduces a hierarchical semi-structured sparse attention framework designed for long-context KV cache compression: 1. **Hierarchical Block + Element Masking:** Keeps critical blocks (attention sinks, local context windows) dense while applying $N:M$ semi-structured pruning (e.g., 2:4) to non-critical blocks. 2. **Trans-Both Layout Optimization:** Transposes both attention GEMM stages ($S^T = K \times Q^T$ and $O^T = V^T \times P^T$), positioning offline-pruned $K$ and $V$ matrices as the first operands to directly utilize hardware sparse tensor cores (`mma.sp`). 3. **Paged Memory Compatibility:** Uses a block index mapping scheme with separate non-zero and metadata pools, which aligns closely with vLLM’s existing `PagedAttention` design. --- * **Unstructured Pruning (e.g., MUSTAFAR):** Reduces memory loading bandwidth, but compute remains dense, yielding minimal speedup on compute-bound stages like prefill attention. * **Coarse Token Skipping (e.g., SnapKV, H2O):** Skips entire tokens, which often leads to severe accuracy degradation in complex long-context tasks compared to fine-grained element-level $N:M$ sparsity. --- According to the published paper: * **Speedup:** Achieves up to **1.85× attention speedup in prefill**
label: feature request

title: Plan for enabling mypy in tests directory
body: **Goal:** Enable MyPy static checking in the `/tests` directory. **Implementation:** Move `tests/**` from `--follow-imports skip` to `--follow-imports silent` in [`tools/pre_commit/mypy.py`](../../tools/pre_commit/mypy.py), one directory at a time, **with each PR enforcing the directories it fixed**. Partial: #26533 /cc @hmellor @yewentao256 --- **Note:** Errors below were measured with `mypy --python-version 3.10 --follow-imports silent <dir>` — the target state for each directory. --- `group_files()` iterates `SEPARATE_GROUPS` in **list order** and `break`s on the first prefix match. `"tests"` is the first entry, so every `tests/**` file is claimed by it: A file only gets `follow_imports=silent` by matching **no** entry at all and falling through to the `""` group. Since `"tests"` matches everything under `tests/`, no per-directory removal can ever take effect before `"tests"` itself is removed — which is the very last step. **Sorting `SEPARATE_GROUPS` by longest prefix does not fix this** (verified): with `tests/config` removed, its files still match `tests` and still run with `skip`. Sorting only changes which *skip* group a file lands in, which is cosmetic today. Consequence if the plan is executed as originally written: every PR from 1 through kv-C fixes real errors but enforces none of them, and all of that work is free to regress until the final PR. **PR 0 below fixes the mechanism so that stops being true.** --- Add an allowlist of verified-clean directories, matched **before** `SEPARATE_GROUPS`, that routes files into the `""` group (no `--follow-imports` flag → pyproject's `silent`): In `group_files()`, before the `SEPARATE_GROUPS` loop: Also sort the `SEPARATE_GROUPS` loop by descending path length so sub-directory groups stop being shadowed by their parents. This is cosmetic today (all those groups run at `skip`) but keeps the per-group log labels honest as directories drain. Verified behaviour with `SILENT_GROUPS = ["tests/config", "tests/v1/shutdown"]

title: Real-time request-queue signal (NUM_REQUESTS_RUNNING/WAITING) for external routers
body: I'm working on an external load-balancing router that dispatches across N vLLM engines for RL rollout (the kvc-aware router in [verl](https://github.com/volcengine/verl)), and I'd like a **real-time, low-latency way to read per-engine request-queue state** — `num_requests_running`, `num_requests_waiting`, and ideally a request-lifecycle event stream (admitted → waiting → running → completed) — so the router doesn't have to rely on the Prometheus `/metrics` endpoint, which is seconds stale. This is the specific problem behind it: the router polls `/metrics` to decide where to send each request, but the queue-depth gauges lag reality by seconds, for two stacked reasons — (1) the scrape cadence itself (a 5 s Prometheus poll is typical), and (2) vLLM's own `waiting → running` scheduler transition. We measured it end-to-end on vLLM 0.21.0: at cold start the router's own synchronous inflight counter is non-zero the instant the first request is dispatched, while `num_requests_running`/`num_requests_waiting` stay **0 for ~18 s** (3–4 poll cycles) and then jump to ~18; in steady state running/waiting trail the true dispatch rate by **3–6 s**. For those 18 cold-start seconds the router's overload and queue signals are all 0, so it routes on inflight alone and collapses the first wave onto the first engine; in steady state every routing decision is based on 3–6 s stale depth. **Pitch.** Any of: - a request-lifecycle **event stream** (SSE / WebSocket / gRPC streaming) emitting running/waiting/inflight transitions as they happen, analogous to the existing KV-cache event stream but for request-queue depth; **or** - a dedicated low-latency stats RPC alongside `/metrics` (no Prometheus scrape round-trip / exposition cost); **or at minimum** - a documented primitive so routers can *subscribe* to queue-depth changes instead of polling. Related / adjacent: #49537 (separate problem — KV-cache events emit 0 events for hybrid models — but found while instrumenting the same router against

title: Support KV-cache events & KV-transfer for hybrid-attention models
body: The KV-transfer connector (`--kv-transfer-config`, e.g. mooncake) currently does **not** work for **hybrid-attention** models — models whose `layer_types` mix `full_attention` with `linear_attention` / state-space layers and are flagged `IsHybrid` (e.g. Qwen3.5, which alternates `linear_attention` (GatedDeltaNet) with `full_attention` every 4 layers). It hard-crashes at startup. KV-cache events (`--kv-events-config`), by contrast, **work** for hybrid models on v0.21 (one gotcha around the inflated hybrid `block_size`, noted below). I'm building cache-aware request routing and want to use a KV-transfer connector for KV migration across hybrid-model replicas; the crash blocks that. Matrix (reproduced end-to-end, logs available on request): | vLLM | `--kv-transfer-config` only | `--kv-events-config` only | both | neither (control) | |---|---|---|---|---| | **0.18.0** | 💥 hard crash | 💥 hard crash | 💥 hard crash | ✅ serves | | **0.21.0** | 💥 hard crash | ✅ works (see note below) | 💥 hard crash | ✅ serves | KV-cache events work correctly for hybrid models on v0.21. There is no bug here; this note records one non-obvious behavior so anyone validating hybrid kv-events isn't misled. For an `IsHybrid` model, vLLM aligns the attention page size to be `>=` the mamba page size, which inflates the attention `block_size`. For Qwen3.5-9B this lands at **528 tokens** (log: `Setting attention block size to 528 tokens to ensure that attention page size is >= mamba page size`), vs the standard **16** for a full-attention model. `BlockStored` is emitted only once a full `block_size` worth of tokens is filled (`block_pool.py`, `cache_blocks` path), so: | Model | `layer_types` | attention `block_size` | prompt tokens sent | KV-cache events emitted | |---|---|---|---|---| | `Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507` (standard) | all `full_attention` | 16 | ~48 | **3 × BlockStored** (`group_idx=0`, `block_size=16`) ✅ | | `Qwen3.5-9B` (`IsHybrid`) | `linear_attention` + `full_attention` (interval 4) | **528*

title: Recency-based progressive mixed-precision KV cache
body: I would like to propose a generic recency-based progressive mixed-precision KV cache. Instead of storing the entire KV cache using one uniform format, vLLM would keep recently created KV blocks in a user-selected higher-precision tier and progressively quantize older completed blocks into lower-precision tiers. The feature should **not be hardcoded to BF16 as the highest tier**. The ordered precision policy should be configurable. Examples include: Example percentage-based policies: or, for a cache whose highest selected precision is FP8: New KV entries and the active partially filled tail block would be written into the **first/highest tier selected by the policy**, which may be BF16, FP8, NVFP4, or another supported format. Once a block is complete and crosses a configured age boundary, it could be asynchronously quantized and moved to the next lower-precision pool. This proposal is specifically about using different KV-cache formats **within the same attention layer based on block age**. It is different from layer-wise mixed precision, where different transformer layers use different formats. Long-context KV caches consume a substantial amount of GPU memory. A uniform low-precision KV cache reduces memory usage, but it applies the same precision to recent and old entries. For long-context and agentic workloads, it may be useful to preserve a recent window in the policy's selected highest precision while compressing older context more aggressively. The intended abstraction is not a single special-case mode such as BF16 + FP8 + NVFP4. It is a generic ordered list of storage tiers. For example: - a BF16-based policy can progressively demote blocks into FP8 and NVFP4; - an FP8-based policy can progressively demote blocks into NVFP4; - an NVFP4-based policy could use a future lower-precision storage format when one is supported; - different hardware backends may expose different valid tier combinations. title: Support fast weight updates from disk
body: vLLM currently uses layerwise reloading while updating weights during RL training without recompilation: https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/training/layerwise/#what-is-layerwise-reloading This currently assumes that weights for a given layer are loaded in order because the layerwise reloading logic allocates buffers per layer: https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/training/layerwise/#troubleshooting-excessive-memory-usage There can be excessive memory usage when weights are received out of order. In some use-cases like disaggregated RL, it is desirable to update weights from disk. In this case, it would be good to leverage GPU Direct Storage to directly load weights into GPU memory. Users would like to do something like: However, the current `fastsafetensors` iterator will lead to large temporary memory allocation due to out of order loading. For Qwen 3.5 35B, I saw temporary memory grow to > 40 GB due to the out of order loading issue, with warnings like: I see two options: 1. Provide a different safetensors iterator that uses GDS but is compatible with layerwise reloading, bounding the temporary memory usage in some way 2. Provide a separate path for updating weights from disk that bypasses the current layerwise reloading and can still use the existing fastsafetensors iterator _No response_ _No response_

title: Add Prometheus metrics for the multimodal preprocessing pipeline
body: When serving multimodal models, a non-trivial portion of Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) is spent in the APIServer process *before* the request reaches the engine: downloading media over HTTP/object storage, decoding images/video, resolving multi-modal items, and rendering + tokenizing the prompt. Today this time is invisible. Per the [metrics docs](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/design/metrics/), `arrival_time` starts when tokenization begins, so all of the above is absorbed into TTFT. Operators serving vision/audio/video models cannot answer basic questions: - Is high TTFT caused by slow media downloads, slow CPU decode, or the engine? - Which media type (image/video/audio) dominates preprocessing cost? - How does preprocessing latency scale with the number of media items per request? vLLM exposes rich engine-side metrics (TTFT, queue time, prefill/decode, KV cache, prefix cache, LoRA). However, there is **no metric** for: - media download latency - media decode (`load_bytes`) latency - total `resolve_items` time per request - total preprocessing (render + tokenize) time The broader observability RFC #39979 (OpenTelemetry tracing) mentions "maybe add download for multimodal models" in passing but does not cover the preprocessing pipeline. This is a lighter, Prometheus-first addition that complements that RFC. title: Priority scheduling is not reflected in KV/prefix cache retention under cache pressure
body: I ran a minimal experiment to check whether the `priority` field in vLLM affects only request scheduling, or whether it is also considered by KV/prefix cache management. The result suggests that `priority` works for request scheduling, but does not appear to affect KV/prefix cache retention. Under KV cache pressure, high-priority requests are not protected from losing cached prompt tokens compared with low-priority requests. This may be expected behavior today, but it creates a gap for priority-based serving: high-priority requests can be scheduled earlier while still losing their KV cache benefit under memory pressure. - vLLM version: `0.19.0` - Model: `Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct` - GPU: NVIDIA A800 80GB - Dataset: MMLU validation split - Prefix caching enabled The KV cache was intentionally limited to create cache pressure: GPU KV cache size: 8,192 tokens The experiment has two parts. 1. Scheduling probe I first verified that `priority` affects request scheduling. Setup: - Submit 32 low-priority requests first. - Wait 0.5 seconds. - Submit 8 high-priority requests. - Use streaming completions and record first-token time. - `priority=0` is treated as high priority. - `priority=10` is treated as low priority. Result: high priority first-token range: 1.448s - 1.483s queued low-priority tail first-token range: 2.697s - 2.723s The high-priority requests, despite being submitted later, were scheduled before the tail of the low-priority queue. This confirms that priority scheduling is active. 2. KV/prefix cache retention probe Then I tested whether priority affects cache retention. Each trial has three phases: warm -> pressure -> probe - `warm`: send sentinel prompts A and B to populate prefix/KV cache. - `pressure`: send MMLU filler prompts to create KV cache pressure. - `probe`: send the same sentinel prompts again and inspect `usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`. title: SSE keep-alive comments for idle periods
body: When vLLM streams responses via SSE (`text/event-stream`), there are periods where no data is sent to the client: 1. **Queue wait**: Request sits in scheduler queue waiting for GPU resources 2. **Prefill**: Model processes the input prompt (especially with long contexts) 3. **Generation pause**: Rare cases where the scheduler preempts a request During these periods, the HTTP connection is silent. This causes issues when vLLM sits behind a proxy with a read timeout: - **Cloudflare Tunnel**: 120s proxy read timeout (Enterprise-only configurable) - **NGINX**: `proxy_read_timeout` (default 60s) - **HAProxy**: `timeout server` (default 50s) - **AWS ALB**: Idle timeout (default 60s) - **GCP Load Balancer**: Idle timeout (default 300s) If the idle period exceeds the proxy's timeout, the connection is silently closed, and the client receives an incomplete or failed response. Add periodic SSE keep-alive comments during idle periods. SSE comments (`: keep-alive\n\n`) are part of the SSE spec and are ignored by all SSE parsers. They would be sent during: 1. **While queued**: Before the request starts prefill 2. **During prefill**: While the model processes the prompt 3. **Between tokens**: Rare gap between decode iterations **Configurable interval** The keep-alive logic would be added to the SSE streaming generator in `vllm/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/serving.py`. Pseudocode: 1. **Cloudflare Tunnel users**: Growing number of self-hosted vLLM deployments use Cloudflare Tunnel for secure access 2. **Production deployments**: Any reverse proxy setup can benefit from this 3. **Zero breaking changes**: SSE comments are transparent to all clients 4. **Minimal overhead**: A 14-byte comment every 15 seconds is negligible - [SSE Spec - Comments](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html#sse-comments) - [Cloudflare Proxy Read Timeout](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cache/concepts/edge-cache ttl/) - Similar implementations: OpenAI's API sends periodic comme

title: Support min_tokens in beam search
body: Beam search should support the request-level `min_tokens` parameter. Today, beam search performs EOS handling in its own online/offline search loops instead of going through the standard sampler stopping path. This means `SamplingParams.min_tokens` does not automatically protect beam search from finalizing a beam on EOS before the requested minimum number of generated tokens has been produced. The proposed feature is to add `min_tokens` to `BeamSearchParams`, propagate the OpenAI request field into beam-search params, and suppress EOS beam finalization until the current beam has generated at least `min_tokens` tokens. There is no related / adjacent issues. : D 👍 _No response_ _No response_

title: Support combining multiple speculative decoding methods (e.g. MTP + ngram)
body: Currently --speculative-config accepts a single method. It would be very useful to allow combining multiple speculative decoding methods in a single serving session — specifically, pairing a primary spec method (mtp, draft_model, EAGLE3, DFlash, etc.) with ngram as a secondary layer. The motivation is that these methods are complementary by nature: MTP, EAGLE3, DFlash, draft_model significantly accelerate the base generation speed by drafting semantically coherent tokens, but they provide little benefit on highly repetitive output — structured JSON, tool calls, code boilerplate, repeated schema tokens, etc. ngram is effectively free (zero inference cost, no VRAM overhead) and excels precisely in those repetitive ranges, but contributes nothing to base generation speed on its own. Running them together — the primary method drafting the semantically dense portion, ngram extending the tail in repetitive ranges — would make the two additive rather than redundant, capturing wins from both systems in a single verification pass. _No response_ _No response_

title: Add cache_salt support for Anthropic Messages API
body: Currently, vLLM supports specifying a cache_salt parameter for explicit prompt cache isolation when using the OpenAI-compatible Completions and Chat Completions APIs (as documented [here](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/serving/online_serving/openai_compatible_server/#completions-api)). However, this parameter is not available when interacting with vLLM via the Anthropic Messages API endpoint. This creates a feature gap for users who rely on the Anthropic client/schema but still need deterministic control over prefix caching isolation. I would like the Anthropic Messages API endpoint in vLLM to accept the cache_salt parameter, mirroring the exact same functionality currently available in the OpenAI-compatible server. Specifically: 1. Update the Pydantic request schema for the Anthropic Messages API to accept an optional cache_salt parameter (e.g., str or int). 2. Pass this parameter down to the vllm engine during generation so it interacts with the prefix caching mechanism exactly as it does for the OpenAI routes. The main alternative right now is forcing clients to switch from the Anthropic API format to the OpenAI API format just to utilize cache_salt, which requires significant application-level refactoring for systems deeply integrated with Anthropic's message schemas (e.g., tool calling, specific system prompt handling). - Link to existing OpenAI implementation docs: [vLLM OpenAI Compatible Server - Completions API](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/serving/online_serving/openai_compatible_server/#completions-api) - This is particularly useful in multi-tenant environments where we want to ensure prompt cache isolation between different users or sessions while using the Anthropic API format.

title: Add a 2-bit KV-cache quantisation backend from Together AI
body: Integrate a new INT2 KV-cache quantisation backend. Paper:**OSCAR** ([arXiv:2605.17757](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17757)). Code: https://github.com/FutureMLS-Lab/OSCAR (500+ stars, proved to be working on Qwen3-32B, GLM-4.7-FP8.) Website: https://oscar-quantize.github.io/ vLLM already has TurboQuant, a data-free Hadamard-rotation KV-cache quantizer. Oscar is similar, but has better accuracy. If we apply the most aggresive quantisation method in TurboQuant, (`turboquant_3bit_nc`), the accuracy will drop by 20%. But with Oscar, for Qwen3-32B and GLM-4.7-FP8 respectively, the mean gap to BF16 is −0.02, and +0.27 points while reducing KV memory by ~8× and increasing large-batch throughput by up to ~7×. The main idea is, before applying clipped INT2 scalar quantization, we first apply a per-layer covariance-aware orthogonal rotation to distribute the values evenly, so they can be later de-quantised with higher precision. To use this feature, just need to load the original model checkpoints, and download a small per-layer rotation file (`[head_dim, head_dim]` orthogonal matrices, a few MB), published in the [OSCAR RotationZoo](https://huggingface.co/Zhongzhu/OSCAR-RotationZoo). Paper author: @zzz0906 vLLM maintainer: @mgoin, @robertgshaw2-redhat - We stored rotation matrix for K and V. - Then, we use the same fp16 `(scale, zero)` parameter for each vector. We then store these values by re-using TurboQuant's `TQFullAttentionSpec` in a Combined `[key_packed | value_packed]` slot (72 B/token/kv-head at `head_dim=128`). - We also introuced 3 additional triton kernels for this feature. title: Faster hybrid-SSM decode via input "replay" ring buffer (ReplaySSM)
body: Decode for hybrid models with SSM layers (Mamba2, Gated DeltaNet) is memory-bandwidth-bound: every step reads the recurrent state from HBM, updates it, and writes it back. The state is large (e.g. Mamba2's `(num_heads, head_dim, d_state)` per layer), and the write-back dominates at batch-1 decode. A research fork, **ReplaySSM** (https://github.com/Johnny-Liou/ReplaySSM, based on vLLM `193ce8812`), proposes caching recent SSM *inputs* in a small per-layer ring buffer and "replaying" them to recompute state on demand, rather than writing full state back each step. This trades a small amount of recompute for reduced HBM traffic — the same IO-vs-recompute trade FlashAttention makes — and reports E2E AR decode and speculative-decode throughput gains on H100/B300 (models incl. Nemotron-Nano-4B and Qwen3.5 4B/122B). Two reasons this is interesting for vLLM specifically: 1. **AR decode**: lower memory traffic on the per-step SSM update, which is the bottleneck for hybrid models at low batch sizes. 2. **Speculative decode**: SSM state rollback on draft-token rejection is a known pain point (normally requires checkpointing full state). An input ring buffer + cursor makes rollback cheap — move the cursor and replay. This is a clean fit for a problem hybrid-model spec decode already has. The fork adds opt-in Triton kernels alongside the existing decode path: - Mamba2: parallel to `selective_state_update` in `vllm/model_executor/layers/mamba/ops/` - Gated DeltaNet: parallel to `fused_recurrent` in `vllm/model_executor/layers/fla/ops/` gated behind flags (`--use-replayssm`, `--use-replayssm-spec`, `--replayssm-buffer-len`, `--replayssm-route`). - **Correctness/parity**: numerical parity of replay-recompute vs. stored state, and accuracy on the spec-decode path. (No parity data in the fork yet.) - **TP correctness**: validate TP1 == TP2 outputs. - **Maintenance**: the fork duplicates the decode kernel per architecture (Mamba2 + GDN, AR + spec). Upstreaming would want this unified

title: Propagate OpenTelemetry Spans to IOProcessor for Custom Sub-Span Creation
body: This feature request extends the observability improvements introduced in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43069, which added OpenTelemetry tracing support to the pooling entrypoint. **The Problem:** Currently, vLLM's pooling entrypoint creates spans for preprocessing and postprocessing operations that wrap IOProcessor method calls. However, the span objects are not accessible to the IOProcessor implementations, preventing them from creating custom sub-spans for detailed tracing of their internal operations. **Why it matters:** Some preprocessing and postprocessing steps can take considerable time, especially for complex IOProcessors like the [SegmentationIOProcessor](https://github.com/torchgeo/terratorch/blob/main/terratorch/vllm/plugins/segmentation/segmentation_io_processor.py#L51C7-L51C30) performing operations like: - **Image loading and decoding** (e.g., loading large geospatial imagery) - **Tiling operations** (e.g., splitting images into tiles for inference) - **Reconstruction** (e.g., stitching tiles back together) - **Format conversion** (e.g., saving outputs as GeoTIFF) Without access to the parent span, IOProcessor implementations cannot describe the length of these operation. Pass the OpenTelemetry span objects to IOProcessor implementations via the existing [`PoolingServeContext`](vllm/entrypoints/pooling/typing.py) object with two new optional fields to store preprocessing and postprocessing spans. IOProcessors can now access the span from the context and add additional insights. Following an example of custom IOProcessor that creates a span for the image loading step. Instead of passing vLLM's spans to the IOProcessor, the IOProcessor could create its own independent root spans for tracing its operations. The problem with this approach is that independent spans are not hierarchically linked to vLLM's request spans, making it difficult to: - View the complete end-to-end trace in a single hierarchy - Debug issues that span both vLLM and IOPro

title: Expose LoRA Adapter Cache Residency in vLLM Metrics
body: **Related Issues:** - llm-d/llm-d-router#1500 (Observability and tracing for LoRA adapter routing) The only LoRA-related Prometheus metric vLLM exposes is `vllm:lora_requests_info`. This metric tracks adapters by **request state** (running vs. waiting), not by **cache residency**. When the last request using an adapter finishes, that adapter vanishes from the metric entirely -- even though its weights remain loaded in GPU VRAM or CPU RAM inside the LRU cache. Downstream routing systems (llm-d router, gateway-api-inference-extension) scrape `vllm:lora_requests_info` to populate `ActiveModels` per pod and drive LoRA-affinity scoring. The affinity scorer routes requests to pods that already hold the target adapter. Because the metric drops adapters the instant they become idle, the router cannot distinguish between: 1. A pod with the adapter **warm in GPU cache** (zero load cost). 2. A pod with the adapter **warm in CPU cache** (GPU-upload cost). 3. A pod that has **never seen the adapter** (full disk-load cost). All three appear identical: absent from the metric. The router treats them equally, frequently routing to pods that must load adapters from scratch. This causes unnecessary latency spikes and adapter thrashing. vLLM manages LoRA adapters through a two-level LRU cache in `LRUCacheLoRAModelManager` (`vllm/lora/model_manager.py`): Both caches are `LoRALRUCache` instances (backed by `cachetools.LRUCache` in `vllm/utils/cache.py`), which already track: - Current contents (adapter IDs and models) - Usage ratio (`currsize / maxsize`) - Hit/miss counts (`stat()` method returning `CacheInfo`) - Pinned adapters (protected from eviction) None of this data reaches the metrics layer today. The cache lives on the **worker side** (`LoRAModelRunnerMixin` -> `LRUCacheWorkerLoRAManager` -> `LRUCacheLoRAModelManager`), while metrics are collected on the **engine/scheduler side** (`PrometheusStatLogger`). Data crosses this boundary via `ModelRunnerOutput`, following a pattern alr

title: triton_scaled_mm uses an AMD-tuned fixed tile heuristic — leaves up to 1.82x on NVIDIA H800 (Hopper sm_90)
body: `triton_scaled_mm` (`vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/compressed_tensors/triton_scaled_mm.py`) selects tile sizes with a fixed hand-written heuristic introduced in #11698 ("avg 2.8x speedup for **int8** models"), which was tuned on AMD. It keys only on `M` (four buckets), ignores `N`, and never tunes `num_warps` / `num_stages`. On an NVIDIA H800 (Hopper, sm_90), benchmarking the exact current kernel against a variant that is a **faithful superset** of it — identical int32 accumulation, the same two-step scale epilogue, and the same optional bias add, with the **only** differences being `@triton.autotune` over tile/`num_warps`/`num_stages` (instead of the fixed heuristic) plus L2-friendly grouped program ordering (PID swizzling, as in the abandoned #20163) — shows the fixed heuristic leaves up to **1.82x** on the table in the compute-bound regime (M ≥ 256) for representative W8A8 INT8 GEMM shapes. Outputs are bit-identical (max rel err = 0.0, verified for both the no-bias and with-bias paths), so the gap is purely tile/scheduling, not precision or a simpler kernel. The effect is stable across **two triton versions (3.6.0 and 3.5.0)** and reproduces on L20 (Ada, sm_89) too (peak 1.65x there) — so this is the heuristic, not a version or a single device. Speedup = `current_ms / autotuned_ms` (faithful-superset kernel, bit-identical output). title: Streaming parser engine for tool/reasoning parsers
body: vLLM has dozens of model-specific streaming tool-call and reasoning parsers, each implementing its own incremental tokenization, state tracking, and argument buffering. That's thousands of lines of structurally similar but independently maintained streaming logic, which makes adding new model formats expensive and bugs hard to fix consistently. Reasoning and tool-call parsing are also handled by separate parser instances stitched together at the serving layer - the reasoning parser runs first, then its leftover content is fed to the tool parser. Getting this handoff right is tricky, and the existing parsers handle it inconsistently across model formats. Many of the existing parsers also assume single-token deltas. They can produce incorrect results or degrade to O(n²) when deltas contain multiple tokens, as happens with speculative decoding, MTP, or `stream_interval > 1`. Replace the hand-rolled parsers with a declarative, state-machine-based engine where O(n) complexity, multi-token delta correctness, and unified reasoning+tool parsing are properties of the engine itself instead of things each parser has to implement correctly on its own. The key properties every parser config gets for free from the engine: - **O(n) streaming** - the engine processes each token/character exactly once. No per-parser state machine tuning required to avoid O(n²). - **Chunk-size invariance** - correct output regardless of whether deltas arrive as single tokens or multi-token chunks (speculative decoding, MTP, `stream_interval > 1`). The engine's incremental lexer handles prefix buffering and boundary conditions in one place. - **Token ID + text hybrid parsing** - models increasingly use special tokens to delineate sections (reasoning, tool calls) with text-based content inside. The engine matches on token IDs where available and falls back to text lexing, rather than forcing everything through text. - **Unified reasoning and tool-call parsing** - a single state machine handles the full

title: Explicit cache breakpoints and cache usage accounting in OpenAI-compatible API
body: vLLM's automatic prefix caching (APC) works well but gives users no control over what gets cached and no visibility into cache performance per request. Users migrating from Anthropic's API to self-hosted vLLM lose two things: **1. Explicit cache breakpoints** Anthropic's API lets users mark specific content blocks with `cache_control` to declare "this prefix is static, prioritize caching it." vLLM's APC is all-or-nothing no way to hint which blocks are stable across requests. Under memory pressure, a 500-token tool schema can get evicted in favor of a one-time long user message. There is currently no workaround for this. **2. Cache accounting in responses** Anthropic returns `cache_creation_input_tokens` and `cache_read_input_tokens` in the usage block. vLLM already tracks `num_cached_tokens` internally in `RequestOutput` but doesn't surface the write vs read distinction or expose it in a standard format. Users currently infer cache behavior from `gpu_cache_usage_perc` in the metrics endpoint - indirect and per-request blind. For production systems with large system prompts or tool schemas, both of these matter for cost modeling and debugging cache misses. **Phase 1 - Cache accounting in responses (low risk, ~50 LOC)** `num_cached_tokens` is already populated in `RequestOutput`. Wire it through `serving_chat.py` to the usage response as `cache_read_input_tokens` and `cache_creation_input_tokens`. Distinguishing writes from reads requires checking whether the block hash already existed in the pool at request time vs being written fresh. **Phase 2 - Explicit `cache_control` parsing (medium complexity)** Parse `cache_control` markers on system and message blocks in the OpenAI-compatible request body. Use them to influence block eviction priority - blocks under an explicit marker get pinned as high-priority in the LRU queue (`FreeKVCacheBlockQueue`) rather than evicted under memory pressure. title: Add per-request preemption count to Prometheus histogram
body: `Request.num_preemptions` is incremented in the scheduler on every preemption event, but was never surfaced to per-request metrics. The existing `vllm:num_preemptions` counter only exposes a cumulative engine-level total, giving no visibility into how frequently individual requests are preempted. This PR adds `vllm:request_num_preemptions` — a per-request Prometheus histogram that records preemption count at request completion. - `RequestStateStats`: add `num_preemptions: int = 0`, incremented in `update_from_events` on each `PREEMPTED` event - `FinishedRequestStats`: add `num_preemptions: int = 0`, populated from `RequestStateStats` in `update_from_finished_request` - `PrometheusStatLogger`: define `vllm:request_num_preemptions` histogram and observe per finished request A histogram (not counter) is appropriate here because the value is per-request (bounded, resets per request) rather than monotonically increasing engine-wide. It allows operators to query p50/p99 preemptions per request and bucket by severity. _No response_ _No response_

title: Cascade: Utility-Driven Adaptive k for MoE Speculative Decoding in V1
body: In `vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py`, `num_spec_tokens` is set once at engine init and never changes: `num_lookahead_tokens` flows into `kv_cache_manager.allocate_slots()` which pre-allocates KV slots assuming every request in every batch will use exactly `k` draft tokens. Today, there exists no mechanism to vary `k` per-request or disable speculation for a specific request mid-flight without restarting the engine. This is fine for dense models, however, **for MoE it is actively harmful**. On a dense model, verification overhead is roughly constant because the target model reads all weights regardless of how many draft tokens it verifies. On the other hand, on MoE, every additional draft token activates a different expert subset, so verification data movement scales with `k`, not batch size. At typical math or reasoning acceptance rates, this makes speculation a net loss. Cascade (https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.20675) quantifies this precisely across five MoE models. In `vllm/v1/spec_decode/llm_base_proposer.py`, `propose()` has no per-request state. There is nowhere to track acceptance history, utility, or current `k` per request — the entire batch gets the same `num_spec_tokens`. Upstream [**Cascade** (MLSys 2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.20675) to vLLM V1. Cascade introduces per-request **speculation utility**: Two phases per request — short **test** phase probes k=1..K_max, long **set** phase locks the utility-maximizing K*. If utility < 1.0, speculation is disabled for that request without evicting the draft model. Paper results on H100: worst-case slowdown **54% → 5%**, throughput improvement **7–14%** over static k. Three components need to change: - `per-request state` tracking in the proposer, - `per-request slot allocation` in the scheduler, and - `variable-length draft` handling in the model runner For CUDA graphs, draft inputs will be padded to `K_max` with masked unused positions, consistent with how existing spec-decode graph captures handle variable ba

title: Improving NVFP4 Quantization via Fast and Accurate Sweep on FP8 Block Scale
body: I propose ScaleSweep to improve NVFP4 quantization. The core idea of ScaleSweep is to select an FP8 E4M3 scale by sweeping a small analytically derived range around the base scale, rather than searching over all FP8 scales. A preliminary implementation and corresponding tests are available here: https://github.com/efsotr/nvfp4quant_test On an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU, `ScaleSweep_MSE_round` shows comparable speed to the current vLLM default operator `vllm._custom_ops.scaled_fp4_quant` on an 8192×8192 speed test: about `1.0064×` latency. In a preliminary error test on Gaussian-distributed inputs, it reduces MSE from `0.0171616` to `0.0135951`. Currently, I only have preliminary Triton implementations of the `ScaleSweep*` kernels, and the tests have only been run on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU. I would appreciate further help from the vLLM community to refine these kernels and integrate ScaleSweep into vLLM's NVFP4 quantization path as production-level operators. @potatosalad @tmm1 @wpc @jefp @mgoin, @Isotr0py, @yewentao256 _No response_

title: Replace hard-coded Granite Rapids PCT detection with a generic, root-free path
body: PR [#43270](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43270) adds opt-in NUMA pinning to Intel Priority Core Turbo (PCT) "priority" cores on Xeon 6776P / 6774P / 6962P, gated by a hard-coded SKU table in `vllm/utils/numa_utils.py::_PCT_CAPABLE_SKUS`. The workaround delivered a measurable end-to-end win on DGX B300 (Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-NVFP4, TP=8, 32K/2 prompts, MC=128: total token throughput **46.1k -> 75.8k tok/s, +64.4 %**), but it is intentionally narrow: - New PCT-capable SKUs require a vLLM patch that adds them to the table. - The `cpu_id % stride in (0, 1)` priority-core filter is empirical, not derived from the kernel. - The CPPC `highest_perf` value is hard-coded per SKU (4.6 GHz -> 46, 4.4 GHz -> 44). This issue tracks **removing that workaround** once we have a way to discover PCT priority cores without root and without per-SKU enumeration. Quoting [#43270 (comment by @vadiklyutiy)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43270#issuecomment-4523383323): In a perfect world the Linux scheduler would prefer PCT priority cores when there are fewer hot threads than priority cores, and vLLM wouldn't need to care. Two recent kernels were tested: - `6.8.0-90-generic` (Ubuntu, kernel from Mar 2024) - `6.14.0-37-generic` (Ubuntu, kernel from Mar 2025) Neither preferentially schedules work on PCT priority cores out of the box. The only kernel interface that reports PCT / CLOS membership is `/dev/isst_interface`, used by `intel-speed-select`: There is no unprivileged sysfs path that exposes per-CPU PCT membership. By identifying these dimensions via a one-time 15-second calibration (PCA on a small sample), SpectralQuant applies error correction only where it matters and skips it on the remaining ~96% noise dimensions — achieving better quality *and* better compression simultaneously. **Paper:** "3% Is All You Need: Breaking TurboQuant's Compression Limit via Spectral Structure" — submitted to NeurIPS 2026, arXiv pending. title: Bottleneck-aware expansion for PD disaggregation
body: This is an RFC-style feature request for discussion. I have been reading through the recent PD, KV transfer, and offloading work, and it feels like the next missing step is not replacing PD, but making PD deployments more adaptive when one side becomes the dominant bottleneck. This proposal does **not** replace PD disaggregation. Instead, it builds on the current PD model and asks whether vLLM should identify the dominant bottleneck at runtime and expand the most effective side first. Concretely, the idea is: - keep the current PD architecture - detect whether runtime pressure is mainly on `prefill`, `decode`, or `decode-side KV capacity` - expand the easiest and most effective side first - reduce user-facing contention before relying on stronger competition inside a fixed topology PD already gives an important separation between prefill and decode pools, and KV transfer / request migration / offloading are all moving in the right direction. But even with PD, deployments still seem mostly statically provisioned. That means it is still easy to end up in situations like: - `prefill` is saturated while `decode` is relatively idle - `decode` is saturated while `prefill` is underutilized - `decode-side KV capacity` becomes the dominant bottleneck even when compute is still available - remote KV transfer backlog creates hidden stalls between the two pools So from my perspective, PD solves mixed-pool interference, but not yet dynamic imbalance between the pools. Introduce a bottleneck-aware expansion layer for PD disaggregation. A simple first version could classify runtime pressure into three categories: 1. `Prefill-bound` Prefill-side compute or memory pressure dominates. 2. `Decode-bound` Decode-side token throughput or scheduling pressure dominates. 3. `Decode-KV-bound` Decode-side KV holding capacity dominates, even if decode compute is not yet saturated. title: Performance Tiers: Apple-style hardware requirements for stable inference
body: vLLM tries to support everything — CUDA, ROCm, CPU, Apple Silicon, TPU. The result? Hundreds of configuration flags, cryptic docs, and users spending hours tuning PagedAttention only to get `OutOfMemory` or suboptimal performance. "The project that tries to catch two hares catches neither." vLLM chases both universal compatibility and ease of use — and fails at both for the average user. Stop trying to run everywhere. Start running perfectly where it matters. Just as Apple doesn't support every hardware configuration — but delivers a flawless experience on supported devices — vLLM should define clear, enforceable system requirements. **Minimum** - Requirements: 16 GB VRAM, 32 GB RAM - Context Length: Up to 8K tokens - Use Case: Development, testing **Recommended** - Requirements: 24 GB VRAM, 64 GB RAM - Context Length: Up to 32K tokens - Use Case: Production, single-user **Optimal** - Requirements: 48+ GB VRAM, 128 GB RAM - Context Length: Up to 128K tokens - Use Case: Enterprise, multi-user 1. **Hardware Detection**: On startup, vLLM checks available resources 2. **Tier Assignment**: Automatically selects the appropriate tier 3. **Fixed Parameters**: Each tier has pre-configured PagedAttention settings — no manual tuning 4. **Hard Barrier**: If hardware doesn't meet Minimum tier — **refuse to start** with a clear message: > "Your hardware doesn't meet the minimum requirements (16 GB VRAM required). Consider using transformers for CPU inference or upgrade your GPU." **Before**: "Why does it crash on my 8 GB GPU?" **After**: "Your hardware is below minimum. title: Port Gemma4 vision encoder to MMEncoderAttention with FlashAttention support
body: Gemma4's vision encoder currently runs via HuggingFace `AutoModel.from_config` in eager mode, using SDPA (scaled dot-product attention) for the encoder's self-attention layers. SDPA is quadratic in sequence length, which drives high peak VRAM for large patch counts and limits how many images/frames can be batched in a single encoder call. Porting the Gemma4 vision encoder to vLLM-native layers using `MMEncoderAttention` with FlashAttention support would: - **Reduce peak VRAM** per encoder call (FA is O(N) memory vs O(N^2) for SDPA), allowing larger encoder batch sizes under the same memory budget - **Improve throughput** by leveraging FA's fused kernels instead of PyTorch's generic SDPA path - **Enable CUDA graph capture** for the encoder path (`compile_mm_encoder=True`), which is currently not practical with the HF eager model - **Align with vLLM's direction** for other vision models that already use `MMEncoderAttention` (e.g., Qwen2-VL, Pixtral) **Context**: The recently merged batched encoder PR groups encoder calls across images/frames, improving video throughput 1.7-3.8x. However, the encoder itself still uses HF's SDPA attention. The dynamic batch sizing (`_encoder_max_batch`) exists specifically because SDPA's memory cost makes unbounded batching unsafe. With FA, the memory ceiling would be much higher, enabling larger batches and further throughput gains — especially for high-resolution images (max_soft_tokens=560/1120, which produce 5,040/10,080 patches per image). **Scope**: The encoder consists of standard multi-head self-attention + MLP layers (16 layers for E2B/E4B, 27 for 26B/31B) with 2D RoPE via `pixel_position_ids` and a simple padding mask. title: DeepSeek V4 w4a4 MegaMoE support
body: DeepSeek V4 uses a MoE architecture where expert weights are already quantized to FP4 (w4), but activations in the MegaMoE pre-dispatch stage are still packed into the symmetric buffer as FP8 (E4M3) — one byte per activation value. On Blackwell (SM100), DeepGEMM already supports FP4 activations. The mismatch is wasteful in two ways: 1. **Buffer footprint**: FP8 packing uses 2× the memory that FP4 would require. 2. **Mainloop efficiency**: FP8 activations force the `kind::mxf8f6f4` mainloop (K=32 with padding). FP4 activations unlock the `kind::mxf4` mainloop (K=64 dense), doubling compute density. The goal of this issue is to support packing activations as FP4 (E2M1) in the MegaMoE pre-dispatch stage, turning w4a8 into true w4a4. --- In `_run_mega_moe()`, the current path is: 1. A Triton kernel (`_stage_deepseek_v4_mega_moe_inputs`) quantizes `hidden_states` to FP8 and packs them into the `x` slot of the symmetric buffer, along with `topk_idx` and `topk_weights`. 2. `fp8_fp4_mega_moe` runs the actual MoE computation. The Triton kernel only outputs FP8 — this is a hard constraint. Changing the kernel to output FP4 E2M1 is non-trivial: the scale factor layout for E2M1 is fundamentally different from FP8, not a simple dtype cast. DeepGEMM already has a CUDA implementation of `mega_moe_pre_dispatch()` (`sm100_mega_moe_pre_dispatch.cuh`) that natively supports E2M1 packing. It does the same job as the Triton kernel — quantize and pack activations, route metadata — but outputs FP4 with the correct scale factor layout. The natural fix: in FP4 mode, replace the Triton kernel call with `deep_gemm.mega_moe_pre_dispatch()`. The vendored DeepGEMM in vllm (commit 891d57b, from deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM) is a pybind11 C extension. After checking the relevant files: - `csrc/apis/mega.hpp`: only registers `get_symm_buffer_size_for_mega_moe` and `fp8_fp4_mega_moe` — no `mega_moe_pre_dispatch`. - `csrc/python_api.cpp`: the pybind11 module does not expose this API. - `get_symm_buffer_size_

title: Per-Layer Parallelism Policy
body: PR #36287 introduced TPA (tensor-parallel-size-attention) to vLLM, and review feedback from Lucas Wilkinson — *"the design shouldn't be attention-specific"* — pointed to a more general need: a per-layer parallelism policy that lets layers declare what they are and have the framework resolve their plan. A single function, owned by the framework, that turns a layer's identity into its parallelism plan: Layers consult the resolver in `__init__` instead of reading global TP accessors. A *plan* is whatever the layer needs to make local decisions — its TP width, its rank within that group, its communication backend, etc. The plan schema is open-ended; the call shape stays the same as new fields are added. The plan being a function of the layer is what makes the design non-attention-specific. The resolver doesn't know it's an attention layer — it knows it's *this* layer at *this* prefix and consults config to decide. New strategies (Q-replication, hybrid attention, MTP, future ideas) become resolver-and-config changes, not N-model changes. The mechanism in §2 is one resolver and one plan dataclass. The breadth comes from what the policy declares for which layers. To make the schema concrete, here are illustrative configurations for different model architectures. The exact field names are not part of this RFC's ask — the question is whether the *shape* (named axes, rules with matchers, per-layer-kind plans) covers the architectural patterns we want to support. One attention rule, one MLP rule. Every block matches the same two rules. Every derivative (Mistral, Phi3, NemotronNAS, TeleChat2, GLM) reuses this verbatim. The resolver dispatches by layer kind, which HF config already declares via `hybrid_override_pattern`. No new metadata source needed — the heterogeneity signal already exists in the model config. title: DeepGEMM wheel integration: planned cleanups
body: Tracking issue for cleanups to the vendored DeepGEMM build path. Companion to upstream DeepGEMM's issue https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM/issues/333 vLLM bundles DeepGEMM under `vllm/third_party/deep_gemm/` and ships a `_C.cpython-X.Y-*.so` for every CPython covered by `requires-python`, all side-by-side in the wheel. Python's loader picks the right one at import. The build is in `cmake/external_projects/deepgemm.cmake` and `tools/build_deepgemm_C.py`. This shape was settled on after the single-`_C.abi3.so` approach was tried and reverted (see #41476 / #41512); landed in #41516. **1. Collapse the per-Python `_C` build down to a single `_C.abi3.so`.** Today's per-Python machinery exists because DeepGEMM's binding uses `PYBIND11_MODULE`, which inevitably links private CPython symbols (`_PyObject_GetDictPtr`, `_PyThreadState_UncheckedGet`, etc.) — so the `.so` is Python-version-coupled regardless of file naming. Two paths to fix: - **Upstream switches to `TORCH_LIBRARY` + a pytorch-shim layer** (cf. [[vllm-flash-attention/csrc/common/pytorch_shim.h](https://github.com/vllm-project/flash-attention/blob/main/csrc/common/pytorch_shim.h)](https://github.com/vllm-project/flash-attention/blob/main/csrc/common/pytorch_shim.h)). Preferred. Coordinate with upstream. - **Maintain a binding fork in vLLM** that includes DeepGEMM's `csrc/apis/*.hpp` and registers ops via `TORCH_LIBRARY`. Avoids upstream coordination at the cost of mirroring binding changes when DeepGEMM adds ops. Either path eliminates `tools/build_deepgemm_C.py`, `tools/setup_deepgemm_pythons.sh`, `tools/check_wheel_deepgemm.py`, the per-Python `foreach` in `deepgemm.cmake`, and the DEEPGEMM_PYTHON_INTERPRETERS plumbing in the Dockerfile. **2. AOT-compile DeepGEMM's CUDA kernels.** DeepGEMM currently JIT-compiles its kernels at runtime, which is why we vendor CUTLASS + CCCL + DeepGEMM headers under `vllm/third_party/deep_gemm/include/`. title: Opt-in: stop caching KV blocks after thinking start tokens
body: Reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3, QwQ, etc.) produce `<think>...</think>` tokens whose content varies across requests even for identical prompts. Under prefix caching, these thinking blocks get hashed, cached, and never reused — pure waste of cache capacity that pressures eviction of actually-reusable prompt blocks. Instead of post-hoc cleanup or adding eviction-priority logic, we take the simplest possible path: once the thinking start token sequence is detected during incremental block hashing, we stop computing hashes for subsequent blocks. No hash means `cache_full_blocks` never registers them — they still exist in GPU memory for the current request but don't pollute the shared cache pool. Changes: - `kv_cache_utils.py`: extend `get_request_block_hasher` to accept `thinking_start_token_ids`; the inner closure scans each block and stops hashing once the pattern is found - `request.py`: add `_in_thinking_section` flag per request - `engine/core.py`: wire up token ids from `ReasoningConfig` - `block_pool.py` / `single_type_kv_cache_manager.py`: relax the assumption that `len(block_hashes) >= num_full_blocks` (use min) - `config/cache.py`: new field `strip_thinking_tokens_from_cache` - `config/vllm.py`: validation (requires prefix caching + reasoning parser) - `engine/arg_utils.py`: CLI flag `--strip-thinking-tokens-from-cache` Default off. No behavioral change unless explicitly enabled. Unit tests (`tests/v1/core/test_strip_thinking_cache.py`): - `_find_token_sequence` correctness (7 cases) - block hasher stops at thinking boundary, incremental behavior, multi-token pattern, feature-off passthrough (22 cases) Integration test (cache pressure A/B): Tested on Qwen3-14B, `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.22` (artificially small cache to create eviction pressure), 20 concurrent identical requests with `enable_thinking=true`: | Metric | Feature ON | Feature OFF (baseline) | |--------|:---:|:---:| | prefix_cache_queries | 400 | 400 | | prefix_cache_hits | 304 | 304 | | Hit

title: Add request-level OTel span attribute for cached prefix-cache input tokens
body: vLLM already exposes useful global Prometheus metrics for prefix caching, including `vllm:prefix_cache_hits`, `vllm:prefix_cache_queries`, and cached prompt-token metrics such as `vllm:prompt_tokens_cached`. The V1 request path also carries per-request cached-token information through `RequestOutput.num_cached_tokens`. From the current tracing docs/source, request-level OpenTelemetry spans appear to include prompt/completion token usage and latency attributes, but I could not find an emitted cache-read / cached-token attribute. This makes it difficult for enterprise observability and FinOps systems to correlate prefix-cache savings with individual request traces. I propose adding a request-level OpenTelemetry span attribute for cached input tokens, using the existing per-request `num_cached_tokens` value already available in the V1 output path. Suggested attribute: `gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens` This aligns with the current OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions for cached input tokens and keeps the change isolated to observability/tracing. It would allow trace backends such as Grafana Tempo, Datadog, Honeycomb, Jaeger, or OpenTelemetry Collector pipelines to correlate cached-token savings with request IDs and upstream gateway/tenant metadata without adding high-cardinality tenant labels to Prometheus metrics. 1. Rely only on global Prometheus counters such as `vllm:prefix_cache_hits`, `vllm:prefix_cache_queries`, and `vllm:prompt_tokens_cached`. These are useful for fleet-level monitoring, but they do not directly provide request-level trace correlation. 2. Rely on OpenAI-compatible response usage fields such as `prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`. This helps API clients, but it does not make the cached-token information available inside distributed traces. 3. Add user/API-key labels to Prometheus metrics. This is not desirable because it can create high-cardinality metrics and privacy concerns. A safer design is to emit cached-token count on the reques

body: PR #41613 migrates `mm_encoder_attn` to vLLM IR with three pure backends (`flash_attn`, `triton`, `native`) fully working and tested. Said that, as rightly pointed out by @ProExpertProg, the migration should wait until IR workspace support exists so that all backends including FlashInfer dispatch uniformly via `--kernel-config.ir_op_priority.mm_encoder_attn` - IR op definition with native semantics - Provider implementations for flash_attn and triton - Per-platform priority lists (CUDA, ROCm, XPU) - `IrOpPriorityConfig.mm_encoder_attn` field - Test suite: 205 passed, 32 skipped across dtypes, batch sizes, sequence lengths, and head configurations - E2E inference verified on all three backends FlashInfer cannot be a pure functional IR implementation today because it requires: * A workspace buffer, a 128MB persistent GPU allocation (`torch.zeros(128*1024*1024, dtype=uint8, device="cuda")`) passed to every call, with no IR mechanism for persistent allocations across calls * FP8 quantization state, including per-instance mutable scale buffers (`_fp8_q/k/v_scale`), amax circular history, and dynamic scale recomputation (`_record_amax_and_update_scales`) that mutates on every forward pass The remaining differences are implementation details that an IR impl could handle internally once the above are resolved (good first issues): * CuDNN-specific bucketing including sequence length and batch size padding (`bucket_flashinfer_max_seqlen`, `add_padding_to_seqlens`) for CUDA graph compatibility * An extended signature with `sequence_lengths`, `q_scale/k_scale/v_scale`, `o_data_type`, and `workspace_buffer` parameters not present in the pure op schema * Post-op head dimension slicing, where the FP8 path pads the head dimension for quantization and then slices the output back - <ins>Draft PR:</ins> #41613

title: Polymorphic buffer management for V1 worker (CPU/GPU staged tensors, lower hot-path overhead)
body: This proposes a polymorphic buffer management path for the V1 worker so internal staged tensors can be handled consistently across CPU and GPU, while reducing hot-path overhead from transient buffer work. **Prototype branch:** `masterFoad/vllm:pr-polymorphic-buffers-clean` **Branch URL:** https://github.com/masterFoad/vllm/tree/pr-polymorphic-buffers-clean **Head commit:** `31e0aa38c` The current buffer/staging flow can incur avoidable overhead in decode and input-prep paths due to temporary allocations and host-side staging patterns. A unified buffer abstraction should improve maintainability and reduce per-step overhead in performance-critical paths. - Introduce `DeviceMemoryManager` to centralize staged tensor allocation strategy. - Use polymorphic staged-write tensors via `.device_tensor` instead of GPU-only assumptions. - Keep CPU-compatible and CUDA-compatible staged write paths under one abstraction. - Refactor V1 worker callsites to use the new staged buffer flow. title: MoE Active Expert Management --moe-gpu-prefetch <num>
body: I would like to propose a new feature for vLLM to improve memory efficiency and scalability for sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models: **`--moe-gpu-prefetch <num>`** This feature introduces **expert-level GPU memory management**, allowing only a limited number of experts to reside on GPU while the rest are offloaded to CPU memory. --- Modern MoE models (e.g., Gemma, Mixtral-style architectures) contain a large number of experts per layer (e.g., 128), but only a small subset (e.g., top-8) are activated per token. Current approaches to handle GPU memory constraints include: * Full model residency on GPU (high memory requirement) * Layer-level CPU offload (coarse-grained and inefficient) These approaches do not align well with the fundamental property of MoE: > Activation is sparse at the expert level, not at the layer level. As a result: * GPU memory is wasted on inactive experts * Data movement is excessive when offloading entire layers * Large MoE models cannot efficiently run on limited GPU setups --- Where `<num>` defines the number of expert models that can reside ("hot") on GPU at any time. Execution model: * All expert weights are stored in CPU memory * GPU memory contains: * shared layers * router * a fixed number of `<num>` expert slots * During inference: * If a routed expert is already on GPU → execute directly * If not → load it from CPU into GPU (evicting another expert if needed) This effectively turns GPU into a **hot expert cache**. --- The core of this feature is to introduce a **fixed set of physical GPU expert slots**, and maintain a dynamic mapping between these slots and logical expert IDs. Runtime structures: Where: * A **slot** is a fixed GPU memory region capable of storing one expert’s weights * An **expert ID** is the logical expert index in the MoE model --- 1. Router selects top-k experts per token 2. For each expert: * Check `expert_to_slot` * **Hit** → directly execute using the corresponding GPU slot * **Miss** → trigger load 3. On miss

title: Add cap to --max-model-len auto (auto-fit with upper bound)
body: vLLM already supports `--max-model-len auto`, which is very useful because vLLM can determine the maximum context length that fits the current memory budget after loading the model and profiling memory usage. I would like to request combining this `auto` behavior with a user-defined upper bound. Example: Semantics: _fitted_len_ = maximum context length vLLM can fit in the configured memory budget _effective_max_model_len_ = min(fitted_len, max_model_len_cap) auto is great when the goal is “use as much context as possible”. However, on shared or restricted hardware, this can be undesirable. If a model supports a very large context length, e.g. 1M tokens, auto may consume the available vLLM memory budget for KV cache, leaving less room for other local applications or parallel serving processes. Simply reducing --gpu-memory-utilization or setting a fixed memory budget does not fully solve this. The useful context length depends on model weight size, architecture, KV cache dtype, parallelism, and other runtime details. A small model can consume the same memory budget as a larger model simply by fitting more context. Use the best context length that fits, but never exceed the deployment/product limit. This would be useful for local serving, small-business internal deployments, workstations, and shared GPUs. Since vLLM already has the auto-fit logic and updates the effective max model length internally, this may be a relatively **small code change**: apply an optional cap after the auto-fit value is computed, before finalizing the engine configuration. _Example:_ Desired context is 128k, but it might **not always fit** completely **and** the model has a **much larger max** context limit. **Fixed** --max-model-len vllm serve <model> --max-model-len 131072 This works only if the chosen value fits. If it does not fit, startup fails instead of gracefully falling back to a smaller fitting value. **Plain** --max-model-len auto This is robust, but it may select a context length

title: Support DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base model
body: Currently vLLM can only run with the DSV4 instruct models. Base models are not supported. Supporting base model is important for RL which normally runs with the Base. When trying to run with the Base model, the `RuntimeError` will occur in `fused_moe/layer.py`: **Why this happens:** 1. The vLLM `deepseek_v4.py` loader are built for the **Instruct** format, where the MoE experts are quantized to **FP4** (highly packed/compressed). 2. The **Base** model uses **pure FP8** weights. The tensor shapes, packing, and quantization scales are completely different. 3. When the weight loader tries to copy FP8-shaped data into an FP4-expecting buffer (or applies an FP4 dequantization view to an FP8 tensor), the dimensions don't align, producing the 2048 vs. 16 mismatch. _No response_ _No response_

title: Unfused global scales for microscale quantization
body: Currently, FP4 kernels in vLLM require that global scales from different partitions are fused into a single global scale for the fused weight ([source](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/compressed_tensors/schemes/compressed_tensors_w4a4_nvfp4.py#L105-L113)). This is a reasonable ask from a performance perspective, but complicates upstream PTQ flows such as LLM Compressor and may lead to unnecessary accuracy loss. Specifically, LLM Compressor has to take a performance hit in order to calculate global scales before local scales, and could see better accuracy recovery from more granular global scales (with minimal runtime cost). I propose supporting unfused global scales by utilizing the `Sm90RowOrScalarBroadcast` cutlass template. Each column has a alpha value which are populated from the partition global scales. https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/compare/main...neuralmagic:vllm:kylesayrs/nvfp4-unfused-global-scale?expand=1 * What is the performance cost of loading per-column global scales? * What is the accuracy improve from per-partition global scales? * Any other blockers? _No response_ _No response_

title: Support a node-local external DP mode with a single `vllm serve` and aggregated admin health endpoint
body: as described in [llm-d/guides/wide-ep-lws/experimental-dp-aware at main · llm-d/llm-d](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/tree/main/guides/wide-ep-lws/experimental-dp-aware) , we currently have DP-aware Dp/Ep scheduling in llm-d as experimental, because our launch mechanism does not interact well with K8s service health checking, etc We should instead have a single server launch command in vllm that intersects well with k8s startup and health checking probes Add a new **node-local external DP mode** in `vLLM` with the following behavior: - a single `vllm serve` command runs **one supervisor per node** - that supervisor launches **one child API server per local DP rank** - each child rank still exposes its own endpoint/port, so external routers can target ranks directly - the supervisor exposes an **admin endpoint** for aggregated health/readiness - if **any local rank** fails or is not ready, the admin endpoint reports unhealthy / not ready - when received the `SIGTERM`, admin process will transfer the signal to all children ranks so that everything exits elegantly. In this example: - `8000-8007` are the per-rank endpoints - `7999` is the admin endpoint for `/health`, `/livez`, `/readyz` etc. This keeps the nice part of external DP mode: - one endpoint per rank - rank-aware routing remains possible But it also makes the deployment much more Kubernetes-friendly: - one top-level `vllm serve` - first-class supervision of local ranks - one admin endpoint for probes - clear unhealthy/not-ready behavior when any rank fails Note: If this looks good to current `external` DP mode, we can bind it to `external` instead of creating a new mode. _No response_

title: Add a standardized config extension point for out-of-tree platforms
body: vLLM's config dataclasses currently use strict Pydantic validation (`extra="forbid"`) and rely on native dataclass fields for downstream logic such as config hashing (`get_hash_factors`) and multiprocessing serialization. This makes it difficult for out-of-tree (OOT) hardware/platform integrations to attach platform-specific configuration values in a safe and maintainable way. Today, the available options are all problematic: 1. Relaxing validation with `extra="allow"` is unsafe and does not integrate cleanly with dataclass-based hashing. 2. Runtime schema mutation / metaprogramming is fragile and risky for serialization and long-term maintenance. 3. Manually adding a platform extension field to each config class is safe, but repetitive and easy to miss as new configs are added. I would like to propose a standardized `platform_extra: dict[str, Any]` extension point that is injected centrally by the existing `@config` decorator in `vllm/config/utils.py`. This keeps the change small and consistent while preserving: - strict validation for normal config fields - compatibility with `dataclasses.fields()` - compatibility with `get_hash_factors` - compatibility with `pickle` / multiprocessing - compatibility with inherited config dataclasses A key edge case here is dataclass inheritance. If the shared field is injected naively, subclasses with non-default fields can fail with: The proposal avoids that by: - skipping duplicate injection through MRO inspection - injecting the shared field as keyword-only This gives OOT platforms a single supported place to store platform-specific config values without weakening existing config safety. 1. Add platform_extra manually to each config class. - Safe, but repetitive and easy to forget for future config classes. 2. Use extra="allow" or other dynamic extension approaches. - Too risky for validation, hashing, and serialization. 3. Introduce a separate runtime registry outside config objects. - Avoids touching configs, but makes hashi

title: Gemma4 on Turing GPUs (SM 7.5): all attention backends hit shared memory limits
body: I'd like to share a compatibility finding for awareness: **Gemma4 models cannot currently run on Turing architecture GPUs (SM 7.5, e.g. RTX 2080 Ti) via any available attention backend in vLLM** by default. I understand this is likely an edge case given the age of the hardware, but wanted to document the situation in case it's useful for the project — either for improving error messaging or for considering potential kernel tuning. | Item | Value | |---|---| | **vLLM version** | `0.19.1rc1.dev4` | | **Commit** | [`fa9e680`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/fa9e68022d29c5396dfbb96d13587b6bc1bdb933) | | **GPU** | 2× NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti (22 GB, CC 7.5, Turing) | | **CUDA Driver** | 580.126.18, CUDA 13.0 | | **Python** | 3.12 (Docker) | | **Model** | Gemma4-31B AWQ 4-bit (`google/gemma-4-31b-it`), also reproduced with `cyankiwi/gemma-4-31B-it-AWQ-4bit` | Gemma4's `text_config` specifies `head_dim: 256` (sliding attention) and `global_head_dim: 512` (full attention). This large head dimension causes Triton-based attention kernels to require **96 KB shared memory**, but Turing GPUs have a hardware ceiling of **64 KB per SM**. Meanwhile, non-Triton backends are blocked by other constraints. Here is the status of each backend I tested: | Backend | Stage | Result | |---|---|---| | `FLASH_ATTN` | Startup (auto-excluded) | Requires SM ≥ 8.0; not available on Turing. | | `FLASHINFER` | Startup | `Reason: ['head_size not supported']` — supports `[64, 128, 256]` only ([`flashinfer.py#L388-L390`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/fa9e68022d/vllm/v1/attention/backends/flashinfer.py#L388-L390)), Gemma4 full-attn layers need 512. | | `TRITON_ATTN` | First inference | `OutOfResources: shared memory, Required: 98304, Hardware limit: 65536` — kernel at [`triton_unified_attention.py#L1124`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/fa9e68022d/vllm/v1/attention/ops/triton_unified_attention.py#L1124). | | `FLEX_ATTENTION` | CUDA graph warmup | Same shared memory er

title: Improve error handling when task='classify' is used with decoder-only models (e.g., Qwen, Llama, Mistral)
body: **Title:** Improve error handling when `task='classify'` is used with decoder-only models (e.g., Qwen, Llama, Mistral) **Body:** When initializing an `LLM` instance with `task='classify'` on a **decoder-only causal language model** (such as `Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct`, `meta-llama/Llama-3-8B`, or `mistralai/Mistral-7B-v0.1`), vLLM fails during model loading with a cryptic error: This occurs because: - The `task='classify'` option triggers the use of a classification head (`score` layer). - However, standard Causal LM checkpoints (like those from Qwen, Llama, Mistral) **do not contain a `score.weight` parameter**, as they are not trained for sequence classification. - vLLM attempts to construct a model with this missing head and only fails at weight-loading time. > Note: Same issue occurs with `meta-llama/Llama-3-8B`, `mistralai/Mistral-7B-v0.1`, etc. vLLM should **validate compatibility between `task` and model architecture early** (e.g., in `LLM.__init__` or engine args parsing) and raise a clear, actionable error such as: Check the model’s architecture before enabling classification mode: Additionally, the documentation for the `task` parameter should explicitly list supported model types. - **vLLM version**: 0.12.0 - **Model**: `Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct` (but affects all Causal LMs) - **Use case**: User mistakenly assumed `task='classify'` works for any model; better guardrails would improve UX. --- Feel free to adjust the tone or add more details, but this version clearly explains the problem, provides reproducible code, proposes a solution, and aligns with vLLM’s goal of being user-friendly and robust. Let me know if you'd like a Chinese version or help submitting it!
